input.description: Read the alternatives and gaps sections

result.output: use calendar versions, 2025.01 onwards, and add Cypher 25. 5.26 is the long-term-support line of the 5.x series.) **Why:** biographical memory is relational. "How's my sister?" is a hop to Maya, then to every memory `ABOUT` her. "Anyone in my family?" is a walk over typed relationships. "What did I believe before?" follows `SUPERSEDES` chains. A vector store can only find text that *looks* similar. Keeping vectors in the same database means one transaction, one consistency model, and one query that can start from a vector hit and continue along edges. Lesson 8 tabulates the needs that vectors alone don't meet. **Costs:** - A second query language (Cypher) and a less common operational skill set. - Neo4j's vector index is good but not a specialist: no BM25 + vector fusion inside the database (the `neo4j-graphrag` Python package's `HybridRetriever` combines a vector and a full-text index in the client). - On 5.26, filters run *after* the approximate search. That's why recall asks for the top 50 and filters by `user` afterwards (see D4). Neo4j 2026.01 added filtering *inside* the vector index (Cypher 25's `SEARCH` clause, with filter properties declared on the index) as a preview. That removes this cost on newer versions. - Community Edition has one user database, no fine-grained access control and no clustering. **Alternatives:** | Option | Wins when | Loses | |---|---|---| | **Vector DB only** (Pinecone, Qdrant, Chroma, pgvector alone) | memory is "find similar past text"; no entities or history | multi-hop, "everything about X", contradiction handling, time | | **Postgres + pgvector** (+ recursive CTEs, or Apache AGE for openCypher) | you already run Postgres; joins are shallow; you want one familiar DB | deep or variable-length traversals get awkward and slow; graph modeling is by convention | | **Another property-graph DB** (Memgraph, FalkorDB, Amazon Neptune; embedded: LadybugDB) | Memgraph: in-memory speed and streaming; FalkorDB: Redis-based, low latency, used by Graphiti and Cognee; Neptune: managed on AWS with LPG and RDF; embedded: no server at all | most speak Cypher or openCypher, so the ideas here carry over, but GDS, APOC and vector-index details differ. Kuzu, the best-known embedded option, was archived in October 2025; LadybugDB is its maintained fork | | **Separate graph DB + vector DB** | each side at large scale, with a specialist team | two writes per memory, no shared transaction, ids to keep in sync | | **RDF triple store** (GraphDB, Stardog, Neptune RDF) + OWL | formal semantics, standard vocabularies, reasoning across organizations | heavier modeling, SPARQL, weaker vector support; overkill for one person's life | | **Document/KV store** (LangGraph `BaseStore`, Redis, Mongo) | a "user profile" document is enough | no relationships; every query is a scan or a custom index | | **Memory framework or service** (Mem0, Zep, Letta, Cognee, LangMem, Neo4j Labs `neo4j-agent-memory`) | you want memory as a product, not a project | less control over identity, time, privacy rules and evaluation; see [Other systems](#how-other-memory-systems-choose) | | **Cloud platform memory** (Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory, Vertex AI Agent Engine Memory Bank) | you already build agents on that cloud; extraction and consolidation are run for you | the provider's extraction rules and scopes; facts are a flat list searched by similarity, with no graph to traverse | | **Files the agent edits** (Anthropic's memory tool, Letta's git-backed MemFS) | the agent should curate its own notes; humans can read and diff them | no index or graph: the agent finds things with file search, and quality depends on the model's discipline | **Revisit when:** you need horizontal scale beyond one machine, hard multi-tenant isolation .... ### D11. Hybrid retrieval: vectors find where to start, the graph reasons from there **Chose:** *hybrid* in sense (b) of the [glossary](glossary.md#hybrid): vector + graph, not vector + keyword. Entities named or *meant* in the message are expanded along `ABOUT` and `RELATED` edges. **Why:** Lesson 6's rule of thumb. Embeddings are good at fuzzy entry points and bad at exact, counted or multi-hop questions. **Costs:** no keyword search, so exact rare words (a medication name, a product code) depend on the embedding model or the name match. **Alternatives:** add a Neo4j full-text (Lucene, BM25-style) index as another retriever and fuse the ranks, for example with reciprocal-rank fusion (Graphiti fuses embedding and BM25 results this way). Neo4j's `neo4j-graphrag` package ships a `HybridRetriever` (vector + full-text). It's a cheap, sensible next step. ### D12. Rank with a transparent formula; use a learned model only to label **Chose:** `rank = 0.6 × similarity + 0.4 × importance/10 × decay` (Lesson 10, the *Generative Agents* recipe, with decay from Lesson 13). Weak matches are **labelled, not dropped**, by a cross-encoder or by the vector score when the embedding model separates well (Lessons 18 and 19). **Why:** every number can be shown in the trace and unit-tested. Dropping weak matches hid an .... --- ## Gaps: what this design does not cover Honest limits, and what would fill each one: | Gap | Risk | What would fill it | |---|---|---| | **Memory poisoning / prompt injection** (OWASP's 2026 Top 10 for agentic applications lists it as ASI06, memory and context poisoning) | Text the user (or a pasted document) says is stored, then returned in future prompts as trusted memory, and it outlives the session | Store provenance and source type; treat memory as data in the prompt; filter instruction-like text at write time; review high-impact memories | | **Scale** | One `User` node becomes a supernode; one Neo4j instance; post-filtered vector search | Partition by user (D4); bucket edges by time; dedicated vector index per tenant; read replicas (Enterprise) | | **Keyword retrieval** | Rare exact words missed by embeddings | Full-text index + rank fusion (D11) | | **Reflection / insights** | No higher-level conclusions ("Alex is happier since moving") | Scheduled LLM reflection writing new `insight` memories with evidence links | | **Procedural memory learning** | The companion doesn't learn *how* to talk to this person beyond boundaries | Store style feedback as memories that edit the persona prompt; review before applying | | **Multimodal memory** | Photos, voice, documents | Embeddings for images/audio, `Media` nodes linked `ABOUT` entities | | **Shared memory across people** | Two users who know the same Maya have two Mayas | Global entity layer with consent; cross-user resolution | | **Erasure outside the graph** | Backups, logs, traces, LLM provider retention | Retention policies, log redaction, provider no-retention settings | | **Cost control** | One extraction call per turn, one remote embedding call per recall | Cheaper extraction model (`LLM_EXTRACTION_MODEL`), batching, caching, skipping more small talk | | **Benchmarks** | Our scenarios aren't comparable with other systems | Run LoCoMo / LongMemEval / BEAM-style suites | | **Learned thresholds** | Hand-measured cut-offs per model | Collect labelled pairs from the trace UI and refit | | **Reasoning memory** | The agent doesn't remember *how* it handled similar requests (which tools, what worked) | Store decision traces as nodes linked to the turn, as Neo4j Labs' `neo4j-agent-memory` does | | **Non-English** | Role-name rules and regexes are English | Language-aware rules; multilingual embedding model (Qwen3 is multilingual) | --- ## How other memory systems choose A compressed comparison, to place this design. Products change quickly: treat this as the shape of each approach, not a feature list. | System | Storage | Who writes memory | Update model | Retrieval | |---|---|---|---|---| | **This tutorial** | Neo4j: graph + vectors | background extractor + end-of-episode pass | supersede, bi-temporal, reinforce | 9 retrievers in code, every turn | | **MemGPT / Letta** | in-context *core* memory blocks + *archival* store + *recall* (conversation history) store; since 2026 optionally a git-backed file tree (MemFS) | the agent itself via tools, and optionally a *sleep-time* agent in the background | agents edit blocks | agent searches when it chooses | | **Mem0** | vector store, optional graph store (Neo4j and others) | LLM extraction pipeline | 1.x: LLM picks ADD / UPDATE / DELETE / NOOP; 2.0 (2026): ADD-only, conflicts resolved at retrieval | vector (+ graph) search | | **Zep / Graphiti** | temporal knowledge graph (Neo4j recommended, FalkorDB and others) | ingestion of *episodes* into entities and fact edges | bi-temporal validity on edges; input.ask: Add the full-text plus vector hybrid retriever?

content.text:
Short answer: for Neo4j, the code imports only the official `neo4j` driver. Every other library the docs name is there for comparison, not as a dependency. The gaps table in [design-decisions.md:518](docs/design-decisions.md:518) lists open work, and none of it has been built yet.

## Libraries the docs mention

| Library | Used? | Why or why not |
|---|---|---|
| **`neo4j`** (official driver) | **Yes** | Every module runs plain Cypher through it. That keeps each query visible, which matters in a tutorial. |
| **GDS and APOC** | **Yes**, but as server plugins, not Python libraries | They're installed in the Docker image ([docker-compose.yml](docker-compose.yml)). Lessons 4 and 15 call them as Cypher procedures (`CALL gds.pageRank...`). The `graphdatascience` Python client isn't used, because it would hide those calls behind Python methods. |
| **`neo4j-graphrag`** (`HybridRetriever`) | No | It comes up in D1 and D11 ([design-decisions.md:73](docs/design-decisions.md:73), [:319](docs/design-decisions.md:319)) as the ready-made way to combine full-text and vector search. Retrieval here is vector + graph, written by hand in [graphrag.py](graphrag.py) and the companion code. `import graphrag` in the code refers to that local file, not this package. |
| **`neo4j-agent-memory`** (Neo4j Labs) | No | It's in the comparison table and in the "Reasoning memory" gap. The project builds the same memory layer itself so you can read it end to end, and the docs note that Labs projects come with no support guarantees. |
| **Graphiti, Mem0, Cognee, Zep, Letta, LangMem** | No | These are memory products. D1 and "How other memory systems choose" use them to place this design. They're dropped for "less control over identity, time, privacy rules and evaluation". Graphiti is called out as the closest relative. |
| **LangGraph `BaseStore`** | No | Neo4j does that job ([glossary.md:59](docs/glossary.md:59)). LangGraph itself is used for the Lesson 7 agent, through `langchain-openai`. |
| **`neosemantics`, RDF and OWL** | No | Lesson 12 uses a lighter ontology instead, written in Python and stored in Neo4j. |

The pattern: tools that run inside the database (GDS, APOC, the vector index) are used. Python wrappers and memory frameworks that would hide the Cypher are not, because showing that Cypher is the point of the course.

## The gaps (not built)

The highest-value ones first:

- **Keyword retrieval.** This is the cheapest gap to close, and D11 calls it "a cheap, sensible next step". You'd add a Neo4j full-text index as one more retriever and merge its ranking with the vector results using reciprocal-rank fusion. `neo4j-graphrag`'s `HybridRetriever` does this out of the box. Writing it by hand would fit the course style better.
- **Memory poisoning.** This is the biggest risk. Nothing records where a memory came from, and nothing filters instruction-like text before it's stored.
- **Reflection / insights** and **reasoning memory.** Both would be new features: a scheduled LLM pass that writes higher-level `insight` memories, and stored decision traces in the style of `neo4j-agent-memory`.
- **Scale, multimodal, shared memory across users, erasure outside the graph, benchmarks (LoCoMo / LongMemEval), learned thresholds, non-English.** These are larger projects than a tutorial change.
Yes, add it

"""Lesson 8 — the memory graph's schema. Safe to run repeatedly (IF NOT EXISTS everywhere).

    (:User:Entity {id, name, kind:'self'})
    (:Entity {id, user, name, kind, aliases, summary, embedding})   embedding: see Lesson 19
        kind: person | pet | place | organization | activity | thing
    (:User|Entity)-[:RELATED {type, said, since, until, updated_at}]->(:Entity)   life graph
        type: canonical ontology type (Lesson 12); said: the word used; until: when it ended
    (:Forgotten {user, episode, embedding})                     tombstone for /forget (Lesson 11)
    (:Memory {id, user, text, kind, importance, embedding,
              occurred_on, due_on, status,                     domain time (when it happened)
              created_at, invalidated_at, last_accessed, access_count})  system time
        kind: fact | preference | event | plan | feeling | boundary
    (:Memory)-[:ABOUT]->(:Entity)                               who/what it concerns
    (:Memory)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(:Memory)                          newer version of a fact
    (:Memory)-[:FROM]->(:Episode)                               provenance
    (:Episode {id, user, started_at, ended_at, summary, mood, embedding})
    (:Episode)-[:NEXT]->(:Episode), (:Episode)-[:HAS_TURN]->(:Turn {idx, role, text, at})
"""
from companion.embeddings import PROFILE

STATEMENTS = [
    "CREATE CONSTRAINT entity_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (e:Entity) REQUIRE e.id IS UNIQUE",
    "CREATE CONSTRAINT memory_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (m:Memory) REQUIRE m.id IS UNIQUE",
    "CREATE CONSTRAINT episode_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (e:Episode) REQUIRE e.id IS UNIQUE",
    "CREATE INDEX memory_user_kind IF NOT EXISTS FOR (m:Memory) ON (m.user, m.kind)",
    "CREATE INDEX entity_user IF NOT EXISTS FOR (e:Entity) ON (e.user)",
    "CREATE INDEX episode_user IF NOT EXISTS FOR (e:Episode) ON (e.user, e.started_at)",
]


def vector_indexes(profile=PROFILE) -> list[str]:
    """One set of vector indexes per embedding model (Lesson 19): memory_vec on n.embedding for
    the default model, memory_vec_<model> on n.embedding_<model> for any other."""
    return [
        f"CREATE VECTOR INDEX {profile.index(name)} IF NOT EXISTS FOR (n:{label}) ON (n.{profile.prop}) "
        f"OPTIONS {{indexConfig: {{`vector.dimensions`: {profile.dims}, "
        f"`vector.similarity_function`: 'cosine'}}}}"
        for name, label in [("memory_vec", "Memory"), ("entity_vec", "Entity"), ("episode_vec", "Episode")]
    ]


def ensure_schema(driver) -> None:
    for stmt in STATEMENTS + vector_indexes():
        driver.execute_query(stmt)
    driver.execute_query("CALL db.awaitIndexes(120)")
        return [f"{r['id']}: {r['name']} ({r['kind']}{', ' + '/'.join(r['rel']) if r['rel'] else ''})"
                + (f" — {r['summary']}" if r["summary"] else "") for r in rows]

    def inferred_relations(self, now: dt.datetime | None = None) -> list[dict]:
        """Relatives the user never linked directly, inferred with the ontology's kinship rules
        (e.g. user -brother-> Leo -daughter-> Ana  =>  Ana is the user's niece_or_nephew).
        Entities protected by a boundary are left out."""
        edges = self._q(
            """
            MATCH (a:Entity {user: $user})-[r:RELATED]->(b:Entity {user: $user}) WHERE r.until IS NULL
              AND """ + visible("r") + """
            RETURN a.id AS src, b.id AS dst, r.type AS type
            """
        )
        found = ontology.infer_kin(edges, self.user)
        if not found:
            return []
        rows = {r["id"]: r for r in self._q(
            """
            MATCH (e:Entity) WHERE e.id IN $ids
              AND NOT EXISTS { MATCH (b:Memory {kind: 'boundary'})-[:ABOUT]->(e) WHERE b.invalidated_at IS NULL AND (b.valid_until IS NULL OR b.valid_until > $now) }
            RETURN e.id AS id, e.name AS name, e.kind AS kind, e.summary AS summary
            """,
            ids=[f["id"] for f in found] + [f["via"] for f in found], now=now,
        )}
        return [{**f, **rows[f["id"]], "via_name": rows[f["via"]]["name"]}
                for f in found if f["id"] in rows and f["via"] in rows]

    @traced("store.recall", "RETRIEVER")
    def recall(self, query: str, k: int = 8, today: dt.date | None = None, touch: bool = True) -> dict:
        """What the companion knows that's relevant to `query`. `touch=False` only looks
        (the web UI's preview): it doesn't count as an access."""
        today = today or dt.date.today()
        now = clock.now_for(today)
        q = partial(self._q, now=now)  # every query below sees the conversation's clock
        vec = embed([query], query=True)[0]  # a message searched against memories (Lesson 19)
        # Core profile: every boundary + the most important stable facts and preferences.
        core = q(
            """
            CALL () {
              MATCH (m:Memory {user: $user, kind: 'boundary'}) WHERE m.invalidated_at IS NULL AND (m.valid_until IS NULL OR m.valid_until > $now)
              RETURN m  // boundaries are never private: every persona respects them
              UNION
              MATCH (m:Memory {user: $user}) WHERE m.invalidated_at IS NULL AND (m.valid_until IS NULL OR m.valid_until > $now)
                AND m.kind IN ['fact', 'preference'] AND m.importance >= 6
                AND NOT coalesce(m.sensitive, false) AND """ + NOT_PROTECTED + """ AND """ + visible("m") + """
              WITH m ORDER BY m.importance DESC, m.created_at DESC LIMIT 8
              RETURN m

            ORDER BY CASE m.kind WHEN 'boundary' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END, m.importance DESC

            WHERE m.user = $user AND m.invalidated_at IS NULL AND (m.valid_until IS NULL OR m.valid_until > $now) AND coalesce(m.status, '') <> 'done'

            WITH hits, reduce(top = 0.0, h IN hits | CASE WHEN h.score > top THEN h.score ELSE top END) AS top

"""Lesson 13 — decay: how relevant a memory still is, as it ages.

Validity (clock.py, `valid_until`) answers "is it still TRUE?". Decay answers "is it still
WORTH BRINGING UP?". They are different: "Riley felt tired" was true on 2026-11-18 forever,
but a month later nobody should mention it.

strength = importance/10 x 0.5 ** (age / half-life of its kind)

- age counts from when it was stored or last CONFIRMED by the user (saying it again resets
  the clock, like spaced repetition). Being recalled does not count: otherwise anything
  recalled once would keep itself alive.
- facts, preferences, boundaries and plans don't decay. A fact doesn't get less true with age;
  it may get STALE, and the companion should check it rather than drop it (see `is_stale`).
- below DORMANT_BELOW a memory is dormant: kept in the graph, left out of recall.
  Milestones (importance >= MILESTONE) never go dormant.

Pure functions, so the curve has unit tests (tests/test_13_time.py).
"""
from __future__ import annotations

HALF_LIFE_DAYS: dict[str, float | None] = {
    "status": 1,       # "at the gym": already expired via valid_until; decays in a day after
    "feeling": 7,      # "tired", "excited about the trip"
    "event": 90,       # "went to a concert"
    "fact": None, "preference": None, "boundary": None, "plan": None,
}
DORMANT_BELOW = 0.05
MILESTONE = 8          # importance at which an event is a life milestone: never dormant
STALE_DAYS = 365       # a fact not confirmed for this long is worth checking
WEIGHT_MATCH, WEIGHT_STRENGTH = 0.6, 0.4


def strength(importance: int, kind: str, age_days: float) -> float:
    half_life = HALF_LIFE_DAYS.get(kind)
    base = importance / 10
    if not half_life or age_days <= 0:
        return base
    return base * 0.5 ** (age_days / half_life)


def is_dormant(importance: int, kind: str, age_days: float) -> bool:
    return importance < MILESTONE and strength(importance, kind, age_days) < DORMANT_BELOW


def rank(score: float, importance: int, kind: str, age_days: float) -> float:
    """Recall order: how well it matches the message, plus how strong it still is."""
    return WEIGHT_MATCH * score + WEIGHT_STRENGTH * strength(importance, kind, age_days)


def is_stale(kind: str, age_days: float) -> bool:
    return kind == "fact" and age_days > STALE_DAYS


def days_until_dormant(importance: int, kind: str) -> float | None:
    """For the lesson's table: how long until a memory stops being recalled."""
    half_life = HALF_LIFE_DAYS.get(kind)
    if not half_life or importance >= MILESTONE:
        return None
    import math
    ratio = DORMANT_BELOW / (importance / 10)
    return 0.0 if ratio >= 1 else half_life * math.log(ratio, 0.5)

# An entity this close to the message (index score) is looked up by the graph hop.

# Keyword search (D11). Embeddings blur rare exact words (a medication name, a product code),
# so a full-text (BM25) search runs beside the vector search. Its hits join the candidates,
# and the two rankings are fused with reciprocal-rank fusion: each list votes 1 / (RRF_K +
# position). Only ranks are combined, never BM25 and cosine scores, which aren't comparable.
# 60 is the constant from the RRF paper (Cormack et al., 2009) and the usual default.
KEYWORD_LIMIT = 20
RRF_K = 60


def keyword_query(text: str, user: str) -> str | None:
    """A Lucene query for the message's words, limited to this user's memories. Lowercasing
    every word means AND / OR / NOT can't act as operators, and \\w+ drops the characters
    Lucene treats as syntax. None when the message has no words ("?!")."""
    words = " ".join(w.lower() for w in re.findall(r"\w+", text))
    if not words:
        return None
    return f'text:({words}) AND user:"{user.replace(chr(92), "").replace(chr(34), "")}"'


def rrf(*rankings: list[str], k: int = RRF_K) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Reciprocal-rank fusion: an id's score is the sum of 1 / (k + position) over the lists
    it appears in (positions start at 1). Being near the top of both lists beats being first
    in only one of them."""
    fused: dict[str, float] = {}
    for ranking in rankings:
        for pos, item in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
            fused[item] = fused.get(item, 0.0) + 1 / (k + pos)
    return fused

"""Lesson 8 — the memory schema. Schema setup must be idempotent: running it twice is a test."""
from companion.schema import ensure_schema
from conftest import rows


def test_schema_is_idempotent_and_complete(driver):
    ensure_schema(driver)
    ensure_schema(driver)  # IF NOT EXISTS everywhere: the second run must not fail
    constraints = {r["name"] for r in rows(driver, "SHOW CONSTRAINTS YIELD name RETURN name")}
    assert {"entity_id", "memory_id", "episode_id"} <= constraints
    indexes = {r["name"]: r["state"] for r in rows(driver, "SHOW INDEXES YIELD name, state RETURN name, state")}
    for name in ["memory_vec", "entity_vec", "episode_vec", "memory_user_kind"]:

Hybrid retrieval: vectors find where to start, the graph reasons from there **Chose:** *hybrid* in sense (b) of the [glossary](glossary.md#hybrid): vector + graph, not vector + keyword. Entities named or *meant* in the message are expanded along `ABOUT` and `RELATED` edges. **Why:** Lesson 6's rule of thumb. Embeddings are good at fuzzy entry points and bad at exact, counted or multi-hop questions. **Costs:** no keyword search, so exact rare words (a medication name, a product code) depend on the embedding model or the name match. **Alternatives:** add a Neo4j full-text (Lucene, BM25-style) index as another retriever and fuse the ranks, for example with reciprocal-rank fusion (Graphiti fuses embedding and BM25 results this way). Neo4j's `neo4j-graphrag` package ships a `HybridRetriever` (vector + full-text). It's a cheap, sensible next step. Graphiti is the closest relative: also a temporal knowledge graph on Neo4j, with episodes as provenance. The main differences here are: - a memory is a sentence node pointing at entities, rather than a fact on an edge; - the explicit relation ontology with rules; - per-persona visibility; - no keyword retrieval (D11). content.text:
Recall now searches memories by their exact words as well as by meaning. That closes the "keyword retrieval" gap, so I removed that row from the gaps table.

**How it works**
- **New index:** `memory_text` is a full-text (BM25) index on the memory's text, with the user id indexed too, in [schema.py](companion/schema.py). Every embedding model uses this one index, because the words don't change when the model does.
- **Recall:** the semantic query in [store.py](companion/store.py) now runs the vector top 50 and the keyword top 20 together. A memory found only by keyword gets its vector score computed directly, so all the existing thresholds (sensitive margin, weak labels, history) still apply to every result.
- **Fusion:** the two rankings are merged by reciprocal-rank fusion. One ranking is the existing match × importance × decay order, the other is BM25. The keyword ranking only reorders: weak matches still go last, so a hit on a common word like "my" can't promote an unrelated memory. Each result now also carries `bm25`, `keyword_rank` and `fused`, and the trace UI shows "words #N".

**Something the tests found**
The user filter inside Lucene isn't exact. The analyzer splits ids on hyphens, so `user:pytest` also matched `user:pytest-crowd`. Results stay correct, because the query checks `m.user` exactly afterwards. The cost is that a user whose id is another id plus a hyphen and a suffix can use up some of the 20 keyword slots. This is documented in `keyword_query` and in D11.

**Tests**
- **Added:** checks on how the search query is built, on the fusion math, and a scenario where another user's memories fill the vector top 50. That last test first confirms the vector search alone misses the memory, then that keyword search finds it.
- **Checked against the old code:** with keyword search switched off, both recall tests fail. In the crowded scenario the memory isn't found at all.
- **Results:** the full default suite passes (215 passed; the 4 skips are tests that need an earlier lesson's step run first).
- **Not run:** the 43 LLM-graded tests, which would show whether the new order changes the end-to-end chat scenarios. I also haven't looked at the trace UI change in a browser.

**Docs updated**
- **D11** now describes the hybrid design and explains why `neo4j-graphrag`'s `HybridRetriever` still isn't used: it hides the Cypher, and it fuses normalized scores where this repo fuses ranks.
- **D1, the glossary, and Lessons 5, 10 and 18** were updated to match.
Do we need to test more or what next ?

Yes, one more round before committing. Two checks are still missing:

1. **The LLM-graded tests (`pytest -m llm`, 43 tests).** These matter most. The change reorders which memories reach the prompt, and only these tests show whether the chat model still answers the scenarios correctly (sensitive recall, boundaries, the "my meds don't help" case). They call your configured LLM endpoint, so they take a few minutes and cost a little in API calls. If something regresses, the likely cause is the keyword vote moving a memory up or down, and the fix would be to weight it lower rather than remove it.
2. **A quick look at the trace UI.** Send one message whose words appear in a memory, and check the "words #N" label in the Vector matches list. This takes about a minute in the in-app browser.

After that:
- **Commit**, with a message like "Add BM25 keyword search to recall, fused with vector ranking by RRF".
- **The next gap: memory poisoning.** It's the highest-risk item left in the gaps table. The first step would be to record where each memory came from (the user, pasted text, or an inference) and to filter instruction-like text when memories are written. That's a change of its own, best done as a separate commit.

I'd run both checks now, starting with the LLM tests.

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?
   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

Rules:
1. Each memory text is ONE standalone third-person sentence using names, never "I"/"you"/"he"

def similarity(a: str, b: str, side: str, scale: str) -> float:
    """side "query": a message against stored text; "cluster": two memories grouped into
    habits (both with the model's clustering instruction); "text": two stored texts."""
    if side == "cluster":
        va, vb = map(np.array, embed_for_clustering([a, b]))
    else:
        va, vb = np.array(embed([a], query=side == "query")[0]), np.array(embed([b])[0])
    cos = float(va @ vb)
    return (1 + cos) / 2 if scale == "score" else cos


def best_cut(yes: list[float], no: list[float]) -> float:
    """The middle of the gap if the two sets separate; else the cut with the fewest mistakes."""
    if min(yes) > max(no):
        return (min(yes) + max(no)) / 2
    cuts = sorted(yes + no)
    return max(cuts, key=lambda c: sum(y >= c for y in yes) + sum(n < c for n in no))


def main() -> None:
    print(f"Model: {PROFILE.model} ({PROFILE.dims} dims)\n")
    suggested = {}
    for name, scale, question, side, pairs in CHECKS:
        yes = [similarity(a, b, side, scale) for ok, a, b in pairs if ok]
        no = [similarity(a, b, side, scale) for ok, a, b in pairs if not ok]
        now = getattr(PROFILE, name)
        right = sum(y >= now for y in yes) + sum(n < now for n in no)
        cut = best_cut(yes, no)
        gap = min(yes) - max(no)
        suggested[name] = round(cut, 3)
        print(f"{name}  ({scale}, {side})  {question}")
        print(f"  yes {min(yes):.3f}-{max(yes):.3f}   no {min(no):.3f}-{max(no):.3f}   "
              f"{'gap' if gap > 0 else 'overlap'} {abs(gap):.3f}")
        print(f"  current {now}: {right}/{len(pairs)} right   suggested {cut:.3f}")
        for ok, a, b in pairs:  # the pairs the current threshold gets wrong
            s = similarity(a, b, side, scale)
            if (s >= now) != ok:
                print(f"    wrong: {s:.3f} {'yes' if ok else 'no '}  {a!r} ~ {b!r}")
        print()
    print("Suggested:", ", ".join(f"{k}={v}" for k, v in suggested.items()))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

CACHE_SIZE = 2048  # names and summaries are embedded again and again during one extraction


def remote() -> bool:
    return bool(config.EMBED_BASE_URL)


def _compute(texts: list[str]) -> np.ndarray:
    global _local, _client
    with _lock:  # the background extractor and the chat can both arrive here first
        if not remote() and _local is None:
            from fastembed import TextEmbedding
            _local = TextEmbedding(PROFILE.model)
        if remote() and _client is None:
            from openai import OpenAI
            _client = OpenAI(base_url=config.EMBED_BASE_URL, api_key=REDACTED,
                             timeout=60, max_retries=3)
    if not remote():
        return np.array(list(_local.embed(texts)), dtype=np.float32)
    out = []
    for i in range(0, len(texts), 64):  # endpoints cap the batch size
        resp = _client.embeddings.create(model=PROFILE.model, input=texts[i:i + 64], encoding_format="float")
        out += [d.embedding for d in sorted(resp.data, key=lambda d: d.index)]
    vecs = np.array(out, dtype=np.float32)
    if vecs.shape[1] != PROFILE.dims:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{PROFILE.model} returned {vecs.shape[1]} dims, expected {PROFILE.dims}")
    return vecs


def embed(texts: list[str], query: bool = False) -> list[list[float]]:
    """Unit-length vectors (so a dot product is the cosine). `query=True`: the text is a message
    searched against stored memories/entities, and gets the model's query instruction."""
    return _embed(texts, PROFILE.query_instruction if query else "")

    """Vectors for grouping memories into habits. Not stored: consolidation embeds again
    when the model has a clustering instruction, else it can use the stored vectors."""
    return _embed(texts, PROFILE.cluster_instruction)


def _embed(texts: list[str], instruction: str) -> list[list[float]]:
    keys = [(instruction, t) for t in texts]
    found: dict[tuple[str, str], np.ndarray] = {}
    with _lock:
        for k in keys:
            if k in _cache:
                found[k] = _cache[k]
                _cache.move_to_end(k)
    missing = [k for k in dict.fromkeys(keys) if k not in found]
    if missing:
        vecs = _compute([i + t for i, t in missing])
        vecs /= np.maximum(np.linalg.norm(vecs, axis=1, keepdims=True), 1e-12)  # an all-zero vector stays zero
        found.update(zip(missing, vecs))
        with _lock:
            _cache.update(zip(missing, vecs))
            while len(_cache) > CACHE_SIZE:
                _cache.popitem(last=False)
    return [found[k].tolist() for k in keys]

content.text:
Yes, there is one, and today's bugs are all symptoms of it.

## The design flaw

**Meaning is stored as prose, and decisions are made by comparing prose against thresholds hand-tuned on hand-written sentences. The prose comes from an LLM that can be swapped at any time.**

The extractor turns a message into a free-text sentence plus a `kind` label. After that, almost every decision is "how similar are these two sentences?" checked against a fixed number. There are about eight such thresholds: duplicate, forgotten, entity match, name match, habit pattern, sensitive floor and margin, entity hop, and the weak-match cut. A few switches also key off `kind` (only `status`/`feeling` get pruned, only some kinds can form habits). So when the extraction model changes how it words or labels things, every one of those decisions can drift silently, and you only find out when a scenario several stages later fails.

Today's failure shows all four ways this goes wrong:

1. **Structure stored as text.** The new model writes dates into the sentence ("…on 2026-11-23"), even though `occurred_on` and `due_on` already hold them. Those date words alone made a dated rock-climbing memory look more like a gym memory than two gym memories looked like each other.
2. **The graph isn't used for identity.** I just checked: all five gym memories are linked only to Riley. No "gym" node exists. In a graph-memory tutorial, "Riley goes to the gym a lot" is still worked out by comparing sentence vectors.
3. **Kind labels act as feature switches.** Gemini filed one visit as `plan`, so the habit feature never saw it. Nothing was wrong except the label choice.
4. **Calibration doesn't match real inputs.** The 0.82 cut was measured on undated, hand-written sentences. It already misclassified one of its own example pairs, and nothing records which extraction model it was measured with.

My in-progress fix (strip dates, lower the cut to 0.804, let plans count) would make the scenario pass. But two of those three changes just tune to Gemini's current wording: the next model change would break it again. Your Qwen3 profile is barely affected (15/15 correct at its current cut), because the weak local model is where this flaw shows first.

## What would fix the class of bugs

1. **Put identity in the graph, not the sentence.** Extraction should link each memory to what it's about, including activities ("gym" as an activity entity), and dates should live only in the date fields, added to the text only for display. Then a habit becomes a Cypher count: at least three memories about the same activity within 60 days, with no similarity threshold. Duplicate detection can work the same way (same entity, same kind, same date) instead of relying on cosine ≥ 0.966.
2. **Calibrate on real extractor output, and record what it was measured on.** Build the calibration pairs from actual scenario runs (`trace_to_case.py` already captures them). Store the extraction model and embedding model each profile was measured with, and have a test fail when either changes. Today, only an embedding-model change prompts re-measuring.
3. **Gate features on properties, not labels.** "Temporary" should mean "has `valid_until`", "dated" should mean "has a date field", and "habit candidate" should mean "linked to an activity". `kind` then becomes a display label rather than a switch.
4. **Test the hand-off between stages.** Extraction tests should check structure: a gym visit links to an activity entity and has a date field. Then drift shows up at the extractor, where it happens, instead of three stages later.

The first item is the real fix and the biggest piece of work: the extraction prompt and schema, a migration for existing memories, and changes to Lessons 9 and 13. The other three are smaller and stop this kind of failure from being silent.

## Where things stand

None of this is committed. The uncommitted changes are: date stripping before clustering, plans counted toward habits, the new tests, and the new calibration pairs (the 0.82 cut is still unchanged). The date stripping is worth keeping either way, since it removes a whole class of noise. The other changes are the per-case patching you want to avoid.

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec. Assume they write idiomatic code in the project's language once they know the exact interface and the exact test, and that they will make a reasonable choice wherever the plan leaves one open. What they cannot know is what you decided: which files, which names and signatures, which values from the spec, which tests prove each task. Document those. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Step Granularity

**Each step is one action with a checkable result:**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

## Review Focus

[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
owns the code, in that task's own step style.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement `function(input: InputType) -> ResultType` in `exact/path/to/file.py`**

One line on the approach when the signature and the test leave a choice
(which library call, which data structure); a code block only for an
algorithm they do not determine.

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## What a Step Contains

A step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing
from it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind
of step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:

- **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the
  spec's exact values in them.
- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the
  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer
  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and
  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.
- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it
  passed.
- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what
  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.

A plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan
longer than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that
decide nothing ("TBD", "handle edge cases", "add appropriate validation",
"write tests for the above", a type or function no task defines) are the
opposite failure, and the self-review catches both.

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.

**5. Proportion:** Compare the plan's length to the spec's. A plan several times longer than the spec it implements is a transcript of the program, not a plan. If code blocks are most of the document, replace bodies with signatures, test names and assertions, and check that each step is still unambiguous.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.

**When no execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**

- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.
- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.

**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?"**

**When an execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Does it capture what you want?"**

**If Subagent-driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development

**If Native chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans

"""What the extraction LLM returns after each exchange (validated with Pydantic)."""
from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

EntityKind = Literal["person", "pet", "place", "organization", "activity", "thing"]
MemoryKind = Literal["fact", "preference", "event", "plan", "feeling", "status", "boundary"]


class EntityOut(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(description="Canonical name, e.g. 'Maya' or 'Portland'")
    kind: EntityKind
    aliases: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list, description="Other names used, e.g. 'my sister'")
    summary: str = Field(default="", description="One short line describing it, e.g. 'the user's cousin, lives in Ohio'")
    ref: str | None = Field(default=None, description="id of the KNOWN entity this is (e.g. 'e_1a2b3c'), or null if it is not known yet")
    new: bool = Field(default=False, description="true if this is a DIFFERENT entity that shares a name with a known one (e.g. a second Sam)")
    corrected: bool = Field(default=False, description="true if the user CORRECTED the name of the known entity in `ref` ('actually it's Maia, not Maya')")


class RelationOut(BaseModel):
    source: str = Field(description="'user' for the user, otherwise an entity name or id")
    target: str = Field(description="An entity name or id")
    type: str = Field(description="canonical type from the list in the instructions, e.g. sister, partner, ex, works_at, lives_in, pet")
    since: str | None = Field(default=None, description="ISO date or year if stated")
    ended: bool = Field(default=False, description="true if this relation has ENDED (breakup, moved away, left a job)")


class MemoryOut(BaseModel):
    text: str = Field(description="Standalone third-person sentence using names, e.g. 'Riley's sister Maya lives in Denver'")
    kind: MemoryKind
    about: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list, description="'user' and/or EVERY entity (name or id) it names, e.g. ['Ana', 'Minecraft']")

# Structure over prose: memory identity in the graph, not in sentence wording

Status: approved direction (2026-11-06), plan in
[`../plans/2026-11-06-structure-over-prose.md`](../plans/2026-11-06-structure-over-prose.md).

## Problem

The extractor turns each message into a free-text sentence plus a `kind` label. Later
decisions then compare sentences by embedding similarity against fixed thresholds, or switch
on `kind`. Those thresholds were calibrated on hand-written sentences, and nothing records
which extraction model produced the text they were tuned for. When the extraction model
changes how it words or labels memories, decisions drift silently, and the failure shows up
stages later.

Observed on 2026-11-06, after switching extraction from `google/gemma-4-31B-it` to
`gemini-3.8-flash` (scenario `situational`, check "three gym visits became one lasting habit"):

1. **Dates in text.** The new model writes `on 2026-11-23` into memory text (rule 2 asks for
   absolute dates in text), though `occurred_on` / `due_on` hold the date. With bge-small, a
   dated rock-climbing memory scored 0.825 against a dated gym memory: higher than gym pairs
   scored against each other (0.78–0.82).
2. **No graph identity.** All five gym memories were `ABOUT` only the user. Rule 10 keeps
   generic activities out of the graph ("those stay in the memory text only"), so habit
   detection had to compare sentences.
3. **`kind` as a switch.** One visit was filed as `plan`. Plans can't join a habit, so only
   two gym memories were eligible.
4. **Calibration doesn't match real inputs.** The 0.82 pattern cut was measured on undated,
   hand-written pairs. It already misclassified one of its own pairs.

## Principle

Where a decision is about *identity* (is this the same activity, is this the same day, is
this temporary), read it from graph structure and typed fields. Use prose similarity only
where meaning really is fuzzy (recall, relevance), and record which models a threshold was
measured with so drift fails loudly.

## Design

### D1. Dates live in fields; text is undated when a field holds the day
- Extraction rule 2 changes: a day that goes into `occurred_on`, `due_on` or `valid_until`
  is **not** written into `text`. Vague anchors with no field ("in the week before
  2026-11-20", "in 2025") stay in text, as now.
- The date is shown from the field wherever memory text is shown to the chat model or the
  user: `format_context` (semantic and graph-hop memories) and the web UI.
- No data migration: the real users have 2 dated texts, both vague anchors with no field.

### D2. Activities someone does are entities
- Rule 10 changes: an activity {user} or someone in their life *does* (the gym, running,
  yoga, therapy, piano lessons) is an entity of kind `activity`, named by its plain noun
  ("gym", "running"), even when unnamed. Every memory about doing it lists it in `about`.
  One-off generic things (a movie, pizza for dinner) still stay text-only.
- Re-mentions resolve through the existing machinery: the prompt's known-entity list and
  `ref` ids, then name/entity matching in `apply()`.

### D3. A habit is a graph count, not a cluster of similar sentences
- `consolidate()` finds habits as: an `activity` entity with occurrence memories `ABOUT` it
  on **at least 3 distinct days** within `PATTERN_WINDOW_DAYS` (60).
- Occurrence memories: `kind IN ['event', 'status', 'plan', 'feeling']`, current, not
  consolidated, not sensitive, not private, and not a `lapsed` plan. ("Occurrence" vs
  "lasting" is what `kind` means, so this gate stays.)
- The day of a memory: `coalesce(occurred_on, due_on, date(valid_until), date(created_at))`.
- The writer LLM (`find_pattern`) still writes the habit sentence or declines. The pattern
  memory is `ABOUT` the activity, and `apply()` also adds `user -practices-> activity`.
- Removed: vector clustering (`_clusters`), `PATTERN_SIMILARITY`, `Profile.pattern`,
  `Profile.cluster_instruction`, `embed_for_clustering`, and the `pattern` calibration check.
- Repeated feelings with no activity ("tired" three times) no longer roll up. Accepted:
  feelings decay, and the old clustering never had a test or scenario for this.

### D4. "Temporary" is a property
- Pruning deletes memories that have **expired** (`valid_until` in the past), are dormant
  and low-importance, instead of `kind IN ['status', 'feeling']`.
- The timeline lists any memory with `occurred_on` or `due_on`, not only events and plans.
- Decay half-lives stay per `kind`: how fast something fades is part of what it is.

### D5. Thresholds record the extraction model they were measured with
- `Profile` gains `extraction_model: str`, the model whose output the thresholds and scenario
  runs were measured on. Both profiles: `google/gemma-4-31B-it` until re-measured.
- Every scenario run includes a check, "thresholds measured with this extraction model",
  that fails when `config.LLM_EXTRACTION_MODEL` differs. The fix: re-run
  `companion.calibrate` and the scenarios on the new model, then update the field.

### D6. The extractor's output structure has its own tests
- LLM evals (`tests/test_11_extraction_evals.py`) check structure, not wording: a gym visit
  is about an `activity` entity named "gym"; a known day is in `occurred_on` and not in the
  text; a one-off dinner creates no entity. Drift shows up at the extractor.

## Out of scope (recorded as gaps)
- Structural duplicate detection (same entity + kind + day) in place of the 0.966 cosine.
- Calibration pairs sampled from real extraction runs instead of hand-written ones.

## Existing data
`uv run python -m companion.reextract --user <name>` re-reads stored conversations with the
new rules. Reinforcing an existing memory already merges its new `ABOUT` links, so activity
links are backfilled without a new migration tool. This writes user data: run it only when
the user says to.

# Structure over Prose Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Make habit detection, date handling and "temporary" decisions read graph structure and typed fields instead of sentence wording, so a change of extraction model can't silently break them.

**Architecture:** Extraction puts known days only in date fields and turns activities into `activity` entities. `consolidate()` finds habits by counting distinct days of memories `ABOUT` one activity, replacing vector clustering. Pruning and the timeline gate on fields. Embedding profiles record the extraction model they were measured with, and every scenario run checks it.

**Tech Stack:** Python 3.12, Neo4j 5.26 (Cypher), Pydantic, LangChain/LangGraph, pytest (`-m llm` for LLM evals), fastembed (bge-small) / remote Qwen3.

**Spec:** [`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-06-structure-over-prose-design.md`](../specs/2026-11-06-structure-over-prose-design.md) (decisions D1–D6 below refer to it)

## Global Constraints

- Run everything with `uv run`. Default tests: `uv run pytest -q` (Neo4j up, local embeddings). LLM evals: `uv run pytest -q -m llm`.
- Tests run on local bge-small unless `TEST_REMOTE_EMBEDDINGS=1` (`tests/conftest.py`): every threshold comes from `PROFILE`, never a literal.
- `PATTERN_WINDOW_DAYS = 60` and `PATTERN_MIN = 3` keep their values; `PATTERN_MIN` now counts **distinct days**.
- The activity relation type is `practices` (existing in `companion/ontology.py`).
- Commit messages: concise, no AI attribution trailers (user's global CLAUDE.md).
- Never run `companion.reextract` against real users (`user:mark`, `user:guest`) without the user's explicit go-ahead.
- Lesson prose follows the repo's style: short declarative sentences, a "why" for each choice, a regression story when a test came from a failure.

## Review Focus

1. **Same activity, different words** ("gym", "the gym", "workout"): the extractor must reuse the known entity via `ref`. Pinned by Task 2's eval `test_a_known_activity_is_reused`.
2. **Several mentions on one day** ("heading to the gym" + "back from the gym" the same afternoon) must not count as three days of habit. Pinned by Task 3's `test_one_day_of_gym_talk_is_not_a_habit`.
3. **A memory about two activities** ("gym then yoga") must count toward both. Pinned by Task 3's `test_a_memory_counts_for_each_activity`.
4. **Private or sensitive occurrences** must never feed a shared pattern (an existing rule the rewritten query must keep). Pinned by Task 3's `test_private_occurrences_dont_form_a_pattern`.
5. **A feeling with no `valid_until`** (extractor omitted it) must not be pruned by the new property gate. Pinned by Task 4's `test_prune_needs_an_expiry`.

---

### Task 0: Start from a clean tree

The uncommitted patch from the debugging session (date stripping before clustering, plans in clusters, calibration pairs) is superseded by this plan.

- [ ] **Step 1:** `git status --short` lists only `companion/embeddings.py`, `companion/store.py`, `companion/calibrate.py`, `tests/test_13_time.py` as modified, plus the untracked `docs/superpowers/`. If anything else is listed, stop and ask.

---

### Task 1: Dates live in fields (D1)

**Files:**
- Modify: `companion/extract.py` (rule 2, rule 3's examples, the Examples block: dated texts lose the date when a field holds it)
- Modify: `companion/store.py` (`recall()` graph-hop memory map, `format_context`)

The plan is written and ready for your review. No code has changed yet.

- **Spec:** [2026-11-06-structure-over-prose-design.md](docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-06-structure-over-prose-design.md) describes the design flaw, the evidence from today's failure, and six decisions.
- **Plan:** [2026-11-06-structure-over-prose.md](docs/superpowers/plans/2026-11-06-structure-over-prose.md) breaks it into eight tasks, each written test-first.

The plan in brief:
- **Task 0:** discard the uncommitted debugging patch; the plan replaces it.
- **Task 1:** keep known days only in the date fields. Memory text stops carrying them, and dates are shown from the fields in the prompt and the UI.
- **Task 2:** activities someone does (the gym, running, yoga) become `activity` entities, and each memory links to the activity it's about. LLM evals check the structure (a gym visit links to "gym"), not the wording.
- **Task 3:** a habit becomes a graph count: at least 3 distinct days of memories about one activity in 60 days. A found habit also adds `user -practices-> gym`. The vector clustering, its threshold, and the clustering instruction are removed. One of the tests uses the exact sentences from today's failure.
- **Task 4:** pruning and the timeline decide from fields (expired `valid_until`, a date present) instead of `kind`.
- **Task 5:** each embedding profile records which extraction model its thresholds were measured with (`google/gemma-4-31B-it` today). Every scenario run fails loudly when the configured model differs.
- **Task 6:** update the docs (Lessons 9, 13 and 19, architecture, design decisions, glossary, README).
- **Task 7:** run the full suite and the LLM suite, re-measure the thresholds on Gemini, then ask you before rewriting your real memories (`reextract` for Mark and guest).

Two trade-offs are written into the spec. Repeated feelings with no activity attached ("tired" three times) will no longer roll up into a habit. Structural duplicate detection and calibration from real extraction runs are listed as gaps rather than included.

Does the plan capture what you want, and which execution approach should we use?
- **Native (my recommendation):** I implement all the tasks in this session, then one fresh reviewer checks the whole branch. Tasks 1–3 depend on each other's interfaces and are each fairly small, so this is the faster path.
- **Subagent-driven:** a fresh subagent implements each task and a separate reviewer checks it before the next one starts. This is more thorough but costs more.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/markcastillo/Library/Application Support/Claude/local-agent-mode-sessions/4b164a4a-f885-4be8-bb7c-2a0b87072585/473e3f37-a4d9-4625-a90c-00c4adb97e89/rpm/REDACTED/skills/executing-plans

# Executing Plans

Execute the plan yourself, task by task, in this session: no implementer
subagent per task, no reviewer per task. One fresh-context review of the
whole branch at the end.

**Why inline:** Subagent-driven development pays for a fresh implementer
and a fresh reviewer on every task, each re-reading the codebase from zero.
Inline execution pays for one context (yours) plus one reviewer at the end.
What it gives up is a fresh context per task and a second pair of eyes per
task. This skill keeps what those two things bought, by other means: the
brief is the spec, the ledger is your memory, TDD is the per-task gate, and
the final reviewer is the second pair of eyes.

**Core principle:** The plan already did the thinking. Execute it exactly,
prove each step with a test you watched fail and then pass, and leave a
record that survives your own forgetting.

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner
between tasks. They chose inline execution to spend less, not to answer
"should I continue?" after every task. Execute all tasks from the plan
without stopping.

**Rulings, not stalls.** Conflicts, ambiguities, plan defects — decide them.
The spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument, and your
judgment settles what neither answers. Record every decision in the ledger
as `Ruling: <what you decided> — <why> — <what it costs if wrong>`, and keep
going. Deviating from the plan without a ledgered ruling is a decision made
in secret.

Four things stop you, and only these: an irreversible or destructive
operation; a security-sensitive action; a side effect outside this worktree
that norms say you ask about first (a merge, a push to a shared branch, a
publish); and a plan so broken that every path forward is a guess. For
those, stop and ask.

## When to Use

- You have a plan from superpowers:writing-plans and your human partner
  chose inline execution at the handoff.
- Your harness has no subagent tool (see the per-platform references in
  `../using-superpowers/references/`). Never fabricate a dispatch; run
  the plan here.
- Tasks are mostly independent — the same precondition as
  superpowers:subagent-driven-development.

A fully specified plan makes inline execution transcription plus testing:
it runs well on a mid-tier session model, and the one place the most
capable model earns its cost is the final review, which this skill
dispatches separately. Tell your human partner so when they choose inline.

Prefer superpowers:subagent-driven-development when your human partner
wants a review gate on every task, or when the plan is long enough that
its later tasks would run on a compacted context. Inline execution over a
long plan still works — the ledger is what makes it recoverable — but the
last tasks get the least of you.

## The Process

```dot

    rankdir=TB;

    subgraph cluster_per_task {
        label="Per Task";
        "task-start: brief + BASE; read the brief" [shape=box];
        "Work the steps in order: TDD, run every verification, read every output" [shape=box];
        "Step output matches plan's Expected?" [shape=diamond];
        "Plan wrong? Rule and ledger. Code wrong? systematic-debugging" [shape=box];
        "Commit as the plan's commit steps say" [shape=box];
        "Completion contract met?" [shape=diamond];
        "task-done: run tests, ledger the result; mark todo complete" [shape=box];
    }

    "Setup: worktree, workspace + ledger, read plan + spec, pre-flight scan" [shape=box];
    "More tasks remain?" [shape=diamond];
    "Final whole-branch review (fresh reviewer if you have one)" [shape=box];
    "Re-grade, then: Critical/Important → ONE fix pass, each fix RED→GREEN + green suite; Minor → ledger" [shape=box];
    "Final review clean: delete this plan's workspace" [shape=box];
    "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch" [shape=box style=filled fillcolor=lightgreen];

    "Plan wrong? Rule and ledger. Code wrong? systematic-debugging" -> "Work the steps in order: TDD, run every verification, read every output";
    "Step output matches plan's Expected?" -> "Commit as the plan's commit steps say" [label="yes, last step"];
    "Commit as the plan's commit steps say" -> "Completion contract met?";

    "Completion contract met?" -> "task-done: run tests, ledger the result; mark todo complete" [label="yes"];
