```

## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. An inline executor that
loses its place re-implements tasks whose commits already exist — the same
failure as a controller re-dispatching them, paid for in your own context.
Track progress in a ledger file, not only in todos. Harness todos are a
live view; the ledger is the record.

The workspace and ledger are shared with superpowers:subagent-driven-development
— same directory, same format — so a plan can change executors mid-flight
and the new one resumes from the same ledger.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run
  `../subagent-driven-development/scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it
  prints the plan's git-ignored directory
  (`<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/`), home to every
  artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, review packages. Another plan's
  directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are
  DONE — do not redo them; resume at the first task without one. Their
  commits exist in git even when your context no longer remembers making
  them: after compaction, trust the ledger and `git log` over your own
  recollection. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file is
  another plan's progress: leave it and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch);
  if that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task. If the plan names a Spec, read that too: the spec is the
authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan resolve
against it. A plan with no reachable spec gets a ledger note saying so —
rulings made without one are provisional.

**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** load superpowers:test-driven-development now,
before Task 1. It governs every step of every task below; a plan whose
steps already say "write the failing test first" does not exempt you
from reading it.

Before Task 1, scan the plan for conflicts between tasks. The plan's
Interfaces blocks tell you where to look: for every task that consumes
what an earlier task produces, one ledger row — the two tasks, what one
produces against what the other consumes, and what you found. Tasks that
share nothing get no row; a plan whose tasks share nothing gets the single
line `Pre-flight: no shared interfaces`. Rule on each conflict a row
surfaces with the spec as the binding authority, record the ruling beside
its row, and start Task 1. Each task's own text is checked when you read
its brief, not here.

## The Task Loop

Everything you print, and every tool result, stays resident in your
context for the rest of the session. Redirect long test output to a file
in the workspace and read its tail; read a brief, not the whole plan.

### 1. Take the task

- Run this skill's `scripts/task-start PLAN_FILE N`. It prints the brief
  path and BASE (the commit the task's range is cut from) in one call.
  Read the brief for every task, including ones you remember from setup:
  what you remember is a summary, the brief has the exact values,
  signatures, and test cases.
- Mark the task's todo in_progress.

Every tool call is a turn that re-reads your whole context. Bookkeeping
rides along with work — a ledger append in the same call as the commit,
never in a call of its own.

### 2. Work the steps

The plan's steps are already in RED-GREEN order; follow them in that
order under superpowers:test-driven-development, loaded at setup. A test
step's code is written first and run first. Watching it fail is a step,
not a formality — a test that passes before the implementation exists is
a finding about the test.

Every step that runs a command has an `Expected:` line. Run the command,
read its output, and compare. Three outcomes:

- **Matches.** Next step.
- **The code is wrong.** Use superpowers:systematic-debugging. Find the
  cause; never patch the symptom to make the step's output match.
- **The plan is wrong** — a step contradicts the spec, an interface from an
  earlier task doesn't match what this task consumes, a command that
  cannot work. Rule on the smallest change that satisfies the spec, ledger
  it as `Task <N>: Ruling: <finding> — <what you decided and why>`, and
  continue. The ruling is carried, not remembered: later tasks that touch
  the same interface read it from the ledger.

Commit as the plan's commit steps say. A task that spans several commits
is fine; BASE is what the review range is cut from, never `HEAD~1`.

### 3. The completion contract

Before a task's ledger line, all of the following are true, with evidence
in this session — not inferred from the diff looking right:

- Every test the brief names exists and ran in this task, and you read
  the output.
- The final test run for the task passed — `task-done` is that run, and
  it writes the command and result into the ledger line.
- Every `Expected:` line in the brief was compared against real output.
- Every deviation from the brief has a `Ruling:` line in the ledger.

**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** superpowers:verification-before-completion governs
the claim. If any item is missing, the task is not complete: finish it.

### 4. Complete the task

Run this skill's `scripts/task-done PLAN_FILE N BASE -- <test command>`
with the test command the brief names for the whole task. It runs the
tests, keeps the full output in the workspace, prints the tail, and — only
if they pass — appends the completion line to the ledger:

`Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, tests: <command> → <result>)`

A failing run records nothing; the task is not complete. When it records,
mark the todo complete and take the next task.

## Final Review

Run `../subagent-driven-development/scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD`
(MERGE_BASE = the commit the branch started from, e.g.
`git merge-base main HEAD`) and review from the file it prints.

**With a subagent tool:** dispatch the reviewer on the most capable
available model — the whole-branch review is a judgment task — using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md), with the
package path, the plan and spec paths, the plan's Review Focus section
verbatim if it has one (the input classes and failure modes the plan's
tests do not exercise — the reviewer checks each deliberately), and a
pointer to the ledger's `Ruling:` lines so it can weigh the calls you
made. Specify the model
explicitly; an omitted model inherits the session's, which may not be the
most capable. This is the one fresh context the whole run buys. Do not
skip it, and do not replace it with your own read of the diff.

**Without a subagent tool:** read code-reviewer.md and perform that review
yourself against the package, as a separate pass after the last task's
ledger line. Write `Final review: self-review (no subagent tool)` to the
ledger, and say so in your final message: a self-review by the author is
weaker than a fresh reviewer, and your human partner decides whether that
is enough before merge.

Sort the findings before you act on any of them. The reviewer's severity
labels are advice; the gate is yours. Its "Declined to judge" list is
yours too: every line there is a ruling you make and ledger, exactly like
a plan conflict — `Final: Ruling: <behavior the reviewer set aside> —
<what a reasonable person using this software gets, and why that stands
or why it is now a finding> — <cost if wrong>`. Re-grade first, by effect: the
spec is a vision document, and a finding's grade is what a reasonable
person using this software gets if it ships, not whether the spec names
the input that triggers it — a reviewer who set a finding at Minor
because the spec was silent has graded the spec, not the effect. Then:

- **Critical and Important** enter the fix pass.
- **Minor** goes to the ledger as `Final: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`
  and to your final message under "Deferred minors". Minors never enter
  the fix pass, and never become rulings — a ruling is a decision about a
  conflict, not a note that you declined a polish suggestion.

Fix the Critical and Important findings yourself — you are the
implementer here — in ONE pass. Each fix is verified by TDD, not by a
second reviewer: write the test that reproduces the finding, watch it
fail, make it pass, then run the whole suite. Record each in the ledger as
`Final: fixed <finding> — <test name> RED→GREEN, suite <N>/<N>`. A fix
without a test that failed first is not verified; a suite that is not
green after the pass means the pass is not over. Do not dispatch a
re-review: it would re-read a diff whose covering tests already answer
"addressed" and whose suite run already answers "broke nothing".

A finding you decide not to fix is a ruling — `Final: Ruling: <finding> —
<why the code stands> — <cost if wrong>` — and reaches your human partner
in the rulings list. There is no second fix pass.

## Finish

Before you delete anything, collect every ledger line containing
`Ruling:` into your final message under "Rulings I made", in the order you
made them, each with what it costs if wrong, and every `minor (deferred)`
line under "Deferred minors". Both lists are exhaustive. Your final
message is the only place the decisions you took on your human partner's
behalf — and the findings you chose not to act on — reach them.

When the final review is clean and its fixes are committed, delete this
plan's workspace directory — the git history is the record now. Sibling
directories belong to other plans; leave them alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "I remember what Task N says" | You remember a summary. The brief has the exact values. Read it. |
| "The plan's code is right, skip watching the test fail" | A test you never saw fail proves nothing. It is one step. Run it. |
| "I'll run the full suite at the end instead of per step" | Per-step runs are how you learn which step broke it. The end-of-task run is the contract, not a substitute. |
| "The plan is wrong here, I'll just do the right thing" | Do the right thing and ledger the ruling. Unledgered deviation is a decision made in secret. |
| "I'll write the ledger lines after a few tasks" | Compaction does not wait for a convenient moment. One line per task, in the same message as the commit. |
| "Let me check in before the next task" | They chose inline to spend less. Progress prompts spend their time instead. Only the four stops stop you. |
| "I read my own diff carefully; the final reviewer is redundant" | Same author, same blind spots. The reviewer is the only fresh context this run buys. |
| "Tests should pass, the change was trivial" | "Should" is not evidence. The contract requires the command and its output. |
| "Subagents are slow and expensive, I'll skip the final review too" | Inline already removed the per-task reviewers. One review of the whole branch is the floor, not the ceiling. |
| "The reviewer said Minor, so it's Minor" | The label graded the spec's silence. Grade what the person gets. Re-grade, then gate. |
| "The fix is obvious, no need for a failing test first" | The failing test is the only proof the finding was real and is now gone. Without it you have a diff and a hope. |
| "I'll fix the minors too while I'm in there" | Every minor you fix is a test, a fix, and a suite run your partner did not ask for. Ledger them; your partner decides. |

# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

**"Other tests" means the project's suite, not just your file.** A
green run of the test you wrote is not a green suite. Before you call
the change done, run the project's test command (bare `pytest`,
`npm test`, `cargo test` — whatever the repo uses) even when your task
named only one test file. A scope statement in your task bounds the
deliverable, not your verification. Any failure that run shows —
including one you didn't cause — goes in your report by name; a red
test you watched scroll past and didn't mention is a report falsified
by omission.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

When writing or changing any test, read [writing-good-tests.md](writing-good-tests.md) for the rules that keep tests honest:
- Name the production change that would make the test fail — before writing it
- Assert on real behavior, never on mock behavior
- Keep test-only code in test utilities, out of production classes
- Understand a dependency's side effects before mocking it

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests written after pass immediately — which proves nothing. They may test the wrong thing, test the implementation instead of the behavior, or miss the edge case you forgot. You never watched it fail, so you never proved it can catch the bug. Test-first forces that failure. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals (spirit not ritual)" | Tests-after answer "what does this do?"; tests-first answer "what should this do?" Tests written after are biased by the code you already wrote — you verify the cases you remembered, not the ones you'd have discovered. Coverage without proof the tests work. |
| "Already manually tested" | Manual testing is ad-hoc: no record of what you covered, no way to re-run it when the code changes, easy to forget cases under pressure. "Worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive. Automated tests run the same way every time. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy — that time is already spent either way. The real choice: rewrite with TDD (high confidence) vs. keep it and bolt tests on after (low confidence, likely bugs). Keeping code you can't trust is the waste. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD IS the pragmatic path: catches bugs before commit, prevents regressions, lets you refactor without fear. "Pragmatic" shortcuts mean debugging in production — slower, not faster. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

result.output:
The ranking used to be a Cypher expression. It's now Python: Cypher fetches the candidates,
`decay.rank()` orders them. **Rules you want to unit-test belong in plain functions.**
`test_strength_halves_every_half_life` is three lines.

## 4. Consolidation — `MemoryStore.consolidate()`

A background job runs after every conversation (`close_episode`) and from `/consolidate`:

1. **Lapse.** Open plans more than 14 days past due become `lapsed`, so the extractor stops
   seeing them as candidates.
2. **Roll up.** Similar short-lived memories (events, statuses, feelings from the last 60
   days) are clustered. Each cluster of 3 or more goes to a small LLM step,
   `extract.find_pattern()`, which writes one lasting memory or declines. The pattern is
   stored through `apply()`, so a pattern seen again is *reinforced*. Each member gets a
   `SUMMARIZES` edge and a `consolidated_at` stamp, and the pattern keeps an `evidence` count.
3. **Prune.** Delete dormant statuses and feelings with importance ≤ 3, but only once they're
   rolled up or older than the 60-day window. Events stay as history even when dormant.

```
✎ + [status] Riley is at the gym before work (until 2026-11-23 15:00)
✎ (upkeep) pattern from 3 memories: + [fact] Riley works out at the gym regularly.
✎ (upkeep) pruned 1 dormant status/feeling memories
```

This is the episodic → semantic step from the [glossary](../docs/glossary.md#semantic)
(*semantic memory*, sense 1: general knowledge, not vector search): many episodes become one
piece of general knowledge. Consolidation finds the episodes to merge with vector similarity
(sense 2), so both senses meet here.

**Clustering uses complete linkage.** A memory joins a cluster only if it's similar to
*every* member, not just one. I measured the threshold rather than guessing it:

```
                                   gym   gym after work   leg day   rock climbing   pizza
Riley is at the gym               1.00        0.91          0.89        0.81         0.69
Riley went to the gym after work  0.91        1.00          0.84        0.82         0.72
Riley is heading to the gym...    0.89        0.84          1.00        0.78         0.65
```

At 0.82, the gym sentences cluster. Rock climbing would chain in through "gym after work"
(0.82) under single linkage, but complete linkage keeps it out (0.78 to "leg day"). The pattern
writer can still decline a cluster that isn't a habit (airport, dentist, post office).

**How the groups are found matters too.** The first version went through memories in time order
and put each into the first group it fit. An early pair could then lock the rest out (see the
results below). `_clusters()` now finds the *largest* all-similar group first, removes it and
repeats. For a few hundred short-lived memories that's still instant.

## What the tests and evals found

- **"places" was used as a relation type.** Asking about "I'm at the airport waiting for my
  flight to Denver" produced `user -places-> Denver`, a *group heading* from the ontology list.
  Group names are now rejected in `normalize()`, and the prompt says they're headings.
- **A trip almost moved the user.** "I'm in Denver for the week" came back with
  `user -lives_in-> Denver`. Because `lives_in` is one-at-a-time (Lesson 12), that would end
  their real home. Adding a prompt *rule* didn't change the output; a prompt *example* did. A
  store guard now also ignores a one-at-a-time relation that only a status mentions.
  Again: let code back up the prompt where a mistake is costly.
- **Pruning ate the pattern.** The first version pruned a minor status after ~2 days, before
  three visits could pile up over a week. It also deleted pattern members, so the scenario's
  "evidence ≥ 3" check failed. Pruning now waits for consolidation or the window, and the
  pattern keeps an `evidence` count.
- **The as-of filter hid the scenarios' memories.** Scenario dates (late November 2026) were
  after the real today, so a default `created_at <= now` made their memories invisible. The
  as-of cut now applies only when a `today` is given.
- **A closed episode whose summary failed was left open**, never linked by `NEXT`. That was a
  code-review leftover, fixed here with a test.

## Concepts and design choices

*Where this fits:* Steps 9 and 13: decay in ranking, validity at read time, consolidation offline. The whole pipeline, step by step, is in [design decisions → the pipeline as concepts](../docs/design-decisions.md#the-pipeline-as-concepts).

**Terms with a specific meaning here** (every sense is in the [glossary](../docs/glossary.md#words-with-several-meanings)):

| Term | Means here | Not to be confused with |
|---|---|---|
| valid time / transaction time | `valid_until`, `occurred_on` / `created_at`, `invalidated_at` | each other (the bi-temporal split) |
| [forget](../docs/glossary.md#forget) | senses 3 and 4: decay ranks lower; pruning deletes trivia | hard delete (sense 1) |
| [semantic](../docs/glossary.md#semantic) | sense 1: consolidation turns repeated *episodic* memories into one *semantic* habit | vector search |
| consolidation | offline: patterns, lapsed plans, pruning | summarizing one conversation |

**Design choices** (with alternatives in [design-decisions.md](../docs/design-decisions.md)):

| We chose | Because | It costs | Instead, you could | |
|---|---|---|---|---|

## Test it — [`tests/test_13_time.py`](../tests/test_13_time.py)

```bash

```

- **Unit:**
  - `parse_until` as a table (date → end of day, missing → 3 hours, past → default);
  - the decay curve and dormancy;
  - "a strong old match still outranks a weak new one".
- **Store, time-travelling with `today=`:**
  - a status is current at noon, *recent* the next day and gone two days later;
  - `memories()` as of a date;
  - a one-day boundary expires;
  - an old minor feeling goes dormant, unless it was confirmed again;
  - an old fact is marked stale;
  - the roll-up, using a **fake pattern writer**;
  - pruning only dormant trivia;
  - plans lapse;
  - a trip doesn't end the real home.
- **LLM evals:**
  - "off to the gym" is a status ending within 6 hours;
  - "tired today" ends today;
  - a week's trip ends within the week and adds no `lives_in`;
  - facts never expire;
  - the pattern writer finds a habit and declines coincidences.

  Every one passed 3 runs out of 3.
- **Scenario `situational`, over five days:**
  1. "Heading to the gym" → a status that expires.
  2. The next day nothing says they're at the gym, and the greeting asks how it went.
  3. "Back from the gym, legs are dead".
  4. "Off to the gym again after work".
  5. "Gym again before work" → a lasting habit with evidence ≥ 3.

`consolidate()` takes the pattern writer as an argument (`writer=find_pattern` in
production, a lambda in tests). **Passing the LLM in** is what lets the clustering, linking
and pruning be tested exactly and for free, while the LLM part gets its own eval.

### Results

Full run: [outputs/13-scenarios.txt](outputs/13-scenarios.txt).

| Suite | Result |
|---|---|
| Fast tests (`pytest -q`, no LLM) | 129 passed |
| Lesson 13 LLM evals, 3 runs each | 6/6 |
| Extraction evals (Lesson 11), `EVAL_TRIALS=3` | 10/10 |
| Scenarios, all 13 | 49/49 (after two fixes, below) |

The habit check failed twice, for two different reasons.

**1. The input didn't contain three visits.** The third gym message was "just got back from
the gym, my legs are dead". The extractor (reasonably) stored it as a *feeling*: "Riley's legs
feel exhausted after a workout". It has no "gym" and is only 0.73 similar to the gym statuses.
Lowering the threshold would have "fixed" it and let unrelated memories chain together.
Instead the scenario got a clearer extra visit ("off to the gym again after work").

**2. Then the clustering lost a group that was there.** On the next run there were four gym
statuses and still no pattern. The first-fit clustering went through them in time order:

```
heading to the gym   + just got back   0.86  -> pair A
going after work     vs just got back  0.80  -> can't join A, starts pair B
at the gym before    vs just got back  0.81  -> can't join A, joins B
```

That makes two pairs and no group of three. Yet heading / after work / before work are 0.85,
0.90 and 0.85 to each other. Finding the largest group first fixed it, and
`test_clustering_finds_the_group_an_early_pair_would_hide` keeps these exact sentences as a
regression test. The full run then gave 49/49, and the gym habit was the only pattern formed in
any scenario:

```
✎ (upkeep) pattern from 3 memories: + [fact] Riley goes to the gym regularly.
```

When a scenario fails, first ask whether the *input* really contained what the check expects.
If it did, the next suspect is an order-dependent shortcut in the code. A real LLM run varies a
little each time, which is how it found a case the fixed fake data in the unit tests never did.

## Takeaways

- Time in memory is three questions: **true?** (validity), **worth mentioning?** (decay),
  **stored this way?** (consolidation). One TTL can't answer all three.
- Make the clock an input. Then time-travel is a parameter, and time-dependent tests are
  deterministic.
- Filter at read time and keep history; delete only on purpose (privacy, trivia), and only
  after consolidation has had its chance.
- Facts don't fade, they go stale: check them instead of dropping them.
- Measure thresholds on real examples, and pick a clustering rule that can't chain.

> **Later, in [Lesson 20](20-growing-the-life-graph.md):** consolidation gets a fourth step that drops entities with no memory and no link left, and edges end when every memory that supported them is retired.

## Next

[Lesson 14](14-production-hardening.md) makes the write path safe for failures and concurrency, and moves extraction to the background.

## 3. Every threshold belongs to a model — [`companion/calibrate.py`](../companion/calibrate.py)

The store makes eight yes/no decisions with a similarity cut-off. Each was measured on
bge-small (the comments in `store.py` keep those measurements). Qwen spreads its scores
differently, so a value that worked for bge-small is wrong for Qwen, and the result fails
quietly: duplicates pile up, two people merge into one, or a habit is never noticed.

So each model has a **Profile** with its own numbers:

```python
Profile("Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B", dims=4096, duplicate=0.966, forgotten=0.89, entity_match=0.94,
        name_match=0.84, pattern=0.665, sensitive_floor=0.655, sensitive_margin=0.015,
        entity_hop=0.62, query_instruction=..., cluster_instruction=...)
```

A model without a profile is refused at startup, with a message pointing here. The numbers

| duplicate (reworded copy) | score | 0.983+ / ≤ 0.964 | 0.977+ / ≤ 0.956 | 0.966 |

Here's what the table says:

- **The better model's scores are lower, not higher.** Qwen puts unrelated pairs far below
  related ones. Floors set for bge-small (0.72, 0.85) would cut off most of Qwen's real matches.
- **The entity hop never worked on bge-small.** Its threshold of 0.85 sits above every
  implicit mention (0.76–0.81), so "how is my kid?" only found Logan through other routes. With
  Qwen at 0.62, the hop finds him. A threshold can look fine for months while it's doing
  nothing, and measuring it is how you find out.
- **Bare names are Qwen's weak spot.** "Ohio" ~ "Iowa" scores 0.854 and "Liz" ~ "Elizabeth"
  scores 0.768. That's tolerable because the name check never decides alone: it runs only after
  the entity match, and nicknames usually arrive as aliases from the extractor.

  climbing" scored 0.77, higher than two gym sentences (0.73). Complete-linkage clustering

```

- the default model keeps the property and index names Lessons 8–18 use, and Qwen gets its own
  4096-dim indexes;
- a model with no measured thresholds is refused;
- a query gets the instruction and stored text doesn't; clustering uses its own instruction;
- vectors are unit length, and repeats come from the cache;
- the active model gets every `duplicate`, `forgotten` and `name_match` calibration pair right,
  except its listed `KNOWN_MISSES` (Qwen: three name pairs, including Bob ~ Robert);
- `reembed` fills in a missing vector, and recall finds that memory again;
- a tombstone with no vector for this model is ignored, not a crash;
- with `weak_below` set, the vector score labels weak matches and the cross-encoder never runs.

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.


Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   - The user's first question was about the gaps mentioned in the docs and the other Neo4j Python libraries the docs mention: are they used, and why or why not. I answered: only the `neo4j` driver is imported. GDS and APOC are server plugins called through Cypher. `neo4j-graphrag`, `neo4j-agent-memory`, Graphiti, Mem0, LangGraph BaseStore and neosemantics are comparison alternatives that aren't used. The gaps table is in docs/design-decisions.md.
   - "Yes, add it": add BM25 keyword search fused with vector search by RRF. Done and committed on main as 1adb511.
   - "Do we need to test more or what next?" and then "Ok continue": I ran the LLM suite and checked the UI. The trace UI was fine, and the commit was made.
   - "Yes, debug it": debug the failing situational scenario check "three gym visits became one lasting habit".
   - The user chose "Count plans (Recommended)" when I asked how plans should be handled.
   - Mid-turn, the user said: "ok so I want to make sure we aren't just playing wack-a-mole fixing bugs in paths that surface. is there some overall design flaw that is generalized and creates these types of bugs we should fix? we don't want to hunt-and-peck at code fixing failing "tests" by coding to each case to fix."
   - "Plan structural fix", then "Native" for the execution method.
   - Mid-run, the user said: "do sub-agents if it makes sense for fresh context reviews".
   - Latest message: "anything else in the codebase that needs similar type of fix?" This needs a text answer listing other places where identity or decisions depend on prose similarity, thresholds or `kind` switches.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Neo4j 5.26: vector indexes (HNSW, post-filtered top 50), a full-text Lucene index (`memory_text` ON EACH [m.text, m.user]), `db.index.fulltext.queryNodes`, `vector.similarity.cosine` (returns 0–1, the same scale as the index score), CALL subqueries with UNION ALL, and COLLECT/COUNT subqueries.
   - Reciprocal-rank fusion: `rrf(*rankings, k=60)`. Weak matches still sort last.
   - The structure-over-prose design: identity lives in graph structure and typed fields, not sentence wording. Activities are `activity` entities. A habit is a Cypher count of memories ABOUT one activity on 3 or more distinct days. Known days live in occurred_on, due_on or valid_until, not in the text. Pruning gates on an expired valid_until. Each embedding `Profile.extraction_model` records the model it was calibrated with, and scenarios run a `threshold_check()`.
   - Embedding profiles: bge-small (local, the test default via conftest) and Qwen3-Embedding-8B (remote; `.env`).
   - LLM extraction runs on gemini-3.8-flash (from `.env`). The thresholds were originally measured with google/gemma-4-31B-it.
   - The superpowers skills in use: systematic-debugging, writing-plans, executing-plans, and test-driven-development. The executing-plans ledger is at `.superpowers/sdd/2026-11-06-structure-over-prose/progress.md`, which is git-ignored.

3. Files and Code Sections:
   - **companion/schema.py** (commit 1adb511): added `"CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX memory_text IF NOT EXISTS FOR (m:Memory) ON EACH [m.text, m.user]"` and an index note in the docstring.
   - **companion/store.py**:
     - 1adb511: added `KEYWORD_LIMIT=20`, `RRF_K=60`, `keyword_query(text, user)` (lowercases words, returns `text:(...) AND user:"<user>"`, or None) and `rrf()`. The semantic recall query gained a CALL{vector top 50 UNION ALL fulltext} branch, `max(score)` and `max(bm25)`, and returns `bm25`. The Python side computes `keyword_rank` and `fused`, and sorts by `(weak, -fused)`.
     - Task 1: the semantic query returns `m.due_on AS due_on`; the graph-hop projection gained `.occurred_on, .due_on`; added `day_note(m)` (" (on X)" or " (due X)"), which is used in the format_context relevant lines.
     - Task 3: removed `_clusters`, `PATTERN_SIMILARITY` and the `embed_for_clustering` import; imports `RelationOut`; `PATTERN_MIN = 3` now counts distinct days.
       ```python
       def _habits(self, now) -> list[dict]:
           MATCH (a:Entity {user:$user, kind:'activity'})<-[:ABOUT]-(m:Memory {user:$user})
           WHERE m.invalidated_at IS NULL AND m.consolidated_at IS NULL
             AND m.kind IN ['event','status','plan','feeling'] AND coalesce(m.status,'') <> 'lapsed'
             AND NOT coalesce(m.sensitive,false) AND NOT coalesce(m.private,false)
             AND m.created_at > $now - duration({days:$days})
             AND NOT coalesce(m.due_on > date($now), false)
           WITH a, m, coalesce(m.occurred_on, m.due_on, date(m.created_at)) AS day ORDER BY m.created_at
           WITH a, collect(m {.id,.text}) AS members, count(DISTINCT day) AS days WHERE days >= $min
           RETURN a.id AS activity, a.name AS name, members,
             COLLECT { MATCH (p:Memory {user:$user})-[:ABOUT]->(a) WHERE p.evidence IS NOT NULL AND p.invalidated_at IS NULL RETURN p.id ORDER BY p.created_at }[0] AS pattern
       ```
       In `consolidate()`: if `h["pattern"]`, call `self._write(lambda: self._summarize([h["pattern"]], h["members"], now))` and log "pattern X gained N memories (name)". Otherwise call the writer, then `_store_pattern(pattern, h, today, now)`. That function sets the pattern's about to `[*(pattern.about or ["user"]), activity id]` and adds `RelationOut(source="user", target=activity id, type="practices")` through `apply()`, then calls `_summarize(self.written_ids, group, now)`. `_summarize` MERGEs SUMMARIZES, sets consolidated_at, and sets `p.evidence = COUNT {(p)-[:SUMMARIZES]->()}`.
     - Task 4: `_prune` uses `m.valid_until IS NOT NULL AND m.valid_until <= $now` (it previously used `kind IN status/feeling`), and its log line is `"pruned {n} dormant expired memories"`. `timeline()` no longer has the kind gate. The consolidate docstring was updated.
   - **companion/extract.py**:

     - The plan example changed to ("Riley is going to Priya's wedding", due_on 2027-06-12).
     - Rule 10 adds that ACTIVITIES {user} or people in their life do, named or not (gym, running, yoga, therapy, piano lessons), are entities of kind activity, named by the plain noun, and EVERY memory about doing one lists it in `about`. One-off generic things stay text-only.
     - The "Off to the gym!" example now includes `entities: gym (activity)` and `about [gym]`.
   - **companion/embeddings.py**: removed `pattern`, `cluster_instruction` and `embed_for_clustering`; added `extraction_model: str = "google/gemma-4-31B-it"`.
   - **companion/calibrate.py**: removed the pattern check and the cluster branch; prints "Measured with extraction model: …".
   - **companion/scenarios.py**: added `import config` and `from companion.embeddings import PROFILE`. `threshold_check()` returns `(f"thresholds measured with this extraction model ({measured} vs {used})", used == measured)`, and `run_scenario` appends it to the results.
   - **companion/static/index.html**:

     - Task 1: added `dayNote(m)` and used it in the semantic and entities renderers.
     - Task 6: the Patterns copy now says "memories about one activity on 3+ days".
   - **Tests**:
     - tests/test_10_recall.py: keyword tests (`keyword_query` params, rrf, rare word XK4471 with a crowd user `user:crowd` of 80 embedded memories plus a vector-miss precondition, `keyword_agreement`, no-words message) and `test_the_day_comes_from_the_field_not_the_text`.
     - tests/test_08: `memory_text` index ONLINE.
     - tests/test_11_extraction_evals.py: `test_a_known_day_goes_in_the_field_not_the_text` (the day may be in any field), `GYM = "e_gym: gym (activity) — Riley's gym workouts"`, `test_a_gym_visit_is_about_the_gym_activity` (3 messages), `test_a_known_activity_is_reused`, `test_a_one_off_dinner_is_not_an_entity`.
     - tests/test_13_time.py: helpers `did()` and `habit()`; tests three_days, one_day, each_activity, wording_does_not_matter, unlinked, lapsed plan, private, future_plans_are_not_days_yet, long_status_counts_on_the_day_it_was_said, known_habit_gathers_new_evidence_without_a_rewrite, shared_members_are_counted_once, prune_needs_an_expiry, an_expired_event_is_pruned_like_a_status; the prune tests were re-seeded with valid_until.
     - tests/test_14_production.py: the pattern test was re-seeded with the gym activity.
     - tests/test_19: removed the cluster-instruction test; added `test_scenarios_check_the_extraction_model`.
   - **Docs** (Task 6): lessons 09, 13 (rewritten consolidation, plus a history of the clustering failure), 19 (pattern row and instruction removed, extraction_model added), 20 (a note); docs/design-decisions.md (new **D22** "Decide identity in the graph; compare prose only where meaning is fuzzy", D1–D22 index, gap rows "Learned thresholds" updated and "Structural dedupe" added; earlier D1/D11 keyword updates); docs/architecture.md (diagrams); docs/glossary.md (pattern and pruning rows; complete-linkage row removed); README (re-measure after changing LLM_EXTRACTION_MODEL); the spec's D3 was amended after review.

input.recap: I found three more places that decide identity from wording or the kind label: duplicate detection, entity matching, and the trip guard. The forget tombstone and the sensitive-recall floor work the same way at lower stakes. Nothing changed yet, and the LLM test run for this branch is still going.

content.text:
Yes. Three more places make the same mistake: they decide whether two things are the same by how the sentence is worded, or by the `kind` label. Two others work the same way, with less at stake.

**Same flaw, worth fixing**

1. **Duplicate detection** ([store.py:660](companion/store.py:660), [store.py:678](companion/store.py:678)). This runs on every memory written. If a new memory's wording is close enough to a stored one (`DUPLICATE_SCORE`), the stored one gets a count bump instead and the new one isn't saved. It already requires the same dates, which helps. But "Alex went running today" and "Alex went swimming today" read alike, and if the extraction model words things differently, the wrong one gets merged and the new fact is lost without any error. **Fix:** only treat it as a duplicate when both memories are about the same entities and have the same kind. Wording similarity then only decides between memories that already match on those. Now that activities are entities, this is cheap to do.

2. **Entity matching** ([store.py:54](companion/store.py:54), [store.py:363](companion/store.py:363)). Deciding whether "Bob" is the same person as "Robert" compares short descriptions the extraction model writes. The calibration run already showed bge getting 3 of the 8 test pairs wrong. The code already does better in one place: [store.py:545](companion/store.py:545) merges "Mom" and "Linda" because a person has only one mother, which is a graph rule, not a wording match. **Fix:** apply that rule more widely. If two entities have the same relation to the user (same coworker, same pet, same city), that counts as evidence they're the same. The description comparison becomes a tiebreaker.

3. **The trip guard** ([store.py:518](companion/store.py:518)). It decides "this is a trip, not a move" by checking `kind == "status"`. The pruning bug we just fixed had exactly this shape. If the model labels "I'm in Denver this week" as an `event`, the trip ends the user's real home. **Fix:** decide by whether the memory has an end time (`valid_until`), as pruning now does. This is the smallest change of the three.

**Same flaw, lower stakes**

4. **Forget tombstone** ([store.py:655](companion/store.py:655)). It decides whether a newly extracted memory is the one the user asked to forget by wording similarity alone. It could also require the same entities.
5. **Sensitive-recall floor.** Sensitive memories come back only when the wording is close enough to the message, and bge gets 3 of the 8 test pairs wrong here too. It could also bring back sensitive memories about entities the message names.
6. **The "step" check** ([store.py:550](companion/store.py:550)). Whether someone is a step-parent is read from the English word "step" in the relation text. It belongs in the relation types as a proper type of its own.

**Fine as they are**

- **Kind checks where kind is the meaning:** decay rates, the core profile (facts and preferences), follow-ups (open plans), and boundaries.
- **Wording similarity where meaning really is fuzzy:** recall, relevance, and entity hops. The new extraction-model check covers these.
- **English-only regexes** (`BOUNDARY_HINT`, `SMALL_TALK`): a separate gap that's already documented.
- **The scenario checks' own `CONTAINS 'gym'` text matches:** these are test assertions, not app logic. They should check for structure ("a pattern about the gym activity"), as I listed in the deferred items.

The LLM test run for this branch hasn't finished yet. Once it does, I'll update `extraction_model` and finish the branch review.

Should I plan items 1–3 as a separate follow-up after this branch? Or should I add just the trip-guard fix (item 3) to this branch now, since it's the same change we made for pruning?

def _name_similarity(a: list[str], b: list[str]) -> float:
    """Best cosine similarity between any name/alias in `a` and any in `b`."""
    va, vb = np.array(embed(a)), np.array(embed(b))
    va /= np.linalg.norm(va, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    vb /= np.linalg.norm(vb, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return float((va @ vb.T).max())


def _similar_names(name: str, known: list[str]) -> bool:
    """Another way to say a known name: "Bob" ~ "Robert", "Robert" in "Robert Smith"."""

    if any(words(name) <= words(k) or words(k) <= words(name) for k in known):
        return True

def forget(self, memory_id: str, today: dt.date | None = None) -> bool:
        """User-requested forgetting: hard delete (privacy beats provenance here).

        The turns that produced it are still in this episode's transcript, and the
        end-of-episode pass would extract it again. So a tombstone keeps only its embedding
        (no text), scoped to that episode, and apply() skips anything that matches it."""
        deleted = bool(self._q(
            """
            MATCH (m:Memory {id: $id, user: $user})
            OPTIONAL MATCH (m)-[:FROM]->(ep:Episode)
            CREATE (t:Forgotten {user: $user, episode: coalesce(ep.id, ''), at: datetime()})
            WITH m, m.id AS id, t
            CALL (m, t) { WITH * WHERE m[$vprop] IS NOT NULL  // none yet if made before a model switch
                          CALL db.create.setNodeVectorProperty(t, $vprop, m[$vprop]) }
            DETACH DELETE m RETURN id
            """,
            id=memory_id,
        ))
        if deleted:  # edges it alone supported go with it
            self._retire_links([(memory_id, None)], today or dt.date.today())
        return deleted

# Structural matching: entities can veto a wording match

Status: approved direction (2026-11-06), follow-up to
[structure over prose](2026-11-06-structure-over-prose-design.md) (D22). Plan in
[`../plans/2026-11-06-structural-matching.md`](../plans/2026-11-06-structural-matching.md).

## Problem

After the structure-over-prose work, three write-path decisions still read identity from
sentence wording or from the `kind` label:

1. **Duplicate detection** (`store._apply`). A new memory whose embedding is within
   `DUPLICATE_SCORE` of a current one (same dates) only reinforces that one and is never saved.
   The check also runs against memories stored earlier in the same extraction. Calibration's
   own NO pairs ("Maya lives in Boston" / "...in Seattle", "went running" / "went swimming")
   depend on the cut alone. If a new extraction model words things more alike, a different
   fact is merged away and lost, and no error is raised.
2. **The forget tombstone** (`store.forget`, `store._tombstones`). Within an episode, a new
   memory whose embedding is within `FORGOTTEN_SCORE` of a forgotten one is dropped. Its NO
   pairs ("Jordan moved to Denver" / "Alex is moving to Denver") are other true things said in
   the same conversation. The same drift drops them.
3. **The trip guard** (`store._apply`). A one-at-a-time relation (`lives_in`) is ignored when
   only a `kind == "status"` memory mentions its target. If the model files "I'm in Denver
   this week" as an `event` with an expiry, the guard misses it and the trip ends the real
   home. Pruning had exactly this flaw and was fixed by reading `valid_until` (D4 of the
   earlier spec).

## Principle

Merging two different things loses data. Splitting one thing into two only leaves a
near-copy. So structure gets a **veto**: wording similarity may decide a match only when the
graph agrees it could be the same thing. Where the graph can't tell, behaviour stays as it is
today.

## Design

### S1. The entity veto
An old memory (stored, stored earlier in this extraction, or a tombstone) can match a new
one only if **every entity the old one is ABOUT, other than the user, is also in the new
one's ABOUT**. The user node never counts.

- "Maya lives in Boston" {Maya, Boston} cannot match "Maya lives in Seattle" {Maya, Seattle}.
- "went running" {running} cannot match "went swimming" {swimming}. Activities are entities
  after D2 of the earlier spec.
- "Logan loves Minecraft" {Logan} still matches the re-read {Logan, Minecraft}, so a
  re-extraction still backfills entities onto the old memory (an existing test).
- Two memories about only the user ("likes coffee" / "likes tea") have nothing to veto with.
  Wording still decides there, as today. That is a stated limit, not a regression.
- If the extractor drops an entity it named before, the new memory is stored as a near-copy
  instead of reinforcing. This is accepted because it's the safe direction.

`kind` is **not** part of the veto. A label slip should not change identity (D22).

### S2. Tombstones carry entities
`forget()` records the forgotten memory's non-user ABOUT entity ids on the `Forgotten` node
(`about`). `_tombstones()` returns each vector with its id set, and S1 applies. A tombstone
with no `about` (made before this change) has an empty set, so it vetoes nothing, which is
today's behaviour.

### S3. "Temporary" for the trip guard is an expiry
The guard's temporary names come from memories with an expiry: `clock.parse_until(...)` is
not None. Lasting names come from memories without one. A status still gets its default
expiry in `clock.parse_until`. That is now the only place `kind` decides "temporary", and
it's the right place, since a status is short by definition.

## Out of scope (recorded)
- **Entity matching** (`resolve_entity`). It is already structural first (the extractor's
  `ref` id, then an exact name or alias). The vector fallback needs both `entity_match` and
  `name_match` to agree, and the one-person-role rule (one mother) merges by graph structure.
  The next step would be relation-aware matching. It is bigger and is not needed for the
  bugs above.
- **The sensitive-recall floor.** Recall is fuzzy by nature (D22 keeps similarity there).
  Recalling sensitive memories about entities the message names is a recall feature, not an
  identity fix.
- **"step" in `r.said`.** This needs a step-relation type in the ontology, which is an
  ontology change.
- **Scenario checks that match text.** Already listed as a deferred minor of the earlier
  plan.

| Extractor lists `supersedes: [id]` | new memory created, old gets `invalidated_at`, `(new)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(old)` |

# Structural Matching Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Wording similarity can no longer merge or drop memories about different entities, and the trip guard reads an expiry instead of `kind`.

**Architecture:** One rule, the *entity veto*, is added in front of the three wording matches in `Store._apply`: the stored duplicate, the repeat within one extraction, and the forget tombstone. An old memory may match only if all its non-user ABOUT entities are in the new memory's ABOUT. Tombstones gain an `about` list. The trip guard sorts names by `clock.parse_until(...)`, not by `kind`.

**Tech Stack:** Python 3, Neo4j 5.26 (Cypher pattern comprehensions), pytest. Use `uv run`.

**Spec:** [`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-06-structural-matching-design.md`](../specs/2026-11-06-structural-matching-design.md)

**Base:** branch off `structure-over-prose` (it needs activity entities and D22) after that branch merges, or on top of it if it hasn't merged yet.

## Global Constraints

- The user node never counts toward the veto (`NOT x:User` in Cypher; drop `self.user` in Python).
- `kind` is not part of the veto (spec S1).
- A tombstone with no `about` vetoes nothing (spec S2): old data behaves as today.
- No threshold values change. Tests that need a wording match set `store_module.DUPLICATE_SCORE` / `FORGOTTEN_SCORE` with `monkeypatch`, so they pass the same way on every embedding model.
- Commit messages are short and technical, with no attribution trailers.

## Review Focus

1. **The extractor dropped an entity on a re-read** (stored {Logan, Minecraft}, new {Logan}). Expected: stored as a near-copy, not reinforced. That's the safe direction. Pinned in Task 1.
2. **User-only memories** ("likes coffee" / "likes tea"). Expected: unchanged, wording decides. Pinned in Task 1 by the existing `test_duplicate_memory_is_reinforced_not_copied`.
3. **A veto hides the nearest memory but a farther, allowed one exists.** Expected: the allowed one still reinforces. The veto must be in the query's WHERE, before `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1`. Pinned in Task 1.
4. **Old tombstones without `about`.** Expected: they still suppress. Pinned in Task 2 by the existing `test_forgotten_memory_is_not_re_extracted_in_the_same_episode`.
5. **A status trip with no explicit `valid_until`.** Expected: still a trip (the status gets its default expiry). Pinned in Task 3 by the existing `test_a_trip_does_not_end_the_real_home`.

---

### Task 1: The entity veto for duplicates and repeats

**Files:**
- Modify: `companion/store.py` (`_apply`, the memory loop at about lines 645–760)
- Test: `tests/test_09_write_path.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Produces: in `_apply`, `about_ids: set[str]` per memory: the non-user entity ids from `mem.about`, resolved with `self._lookup(n, known)` *before* the duplicate checks. `stored` becomes `list[tuple[np.ndarray, set[str]]]`. Task 2 reuses `about_ids`.

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing tests** (in `tests/test_09_write_path.py`)

```python
from companion import store as store_module

MAYA_BOSTON = dict(entities=[EntityOut(name="Maya", kind="person"), EntityOut(name="Boston", kind="place")])

def test_a_wording_match_about_other_entities_is_new(store, monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr(store_module, "DUPLICATE_SCORE", 0.0)  # wording says "same" for anything
    store.apply(Extraction(**MAYA_BOSTON, memories=[mem("Pytest's sister Maya lives in Boston", about=["Maya", "Boston"])]), today=T)
    log = store.apply(Extraction(entities=[EntityOut(name="Maya", kind="person"), EntityOut(name="Seattle", kind="place")],
                                 memories=[mem("Pytest's sister Maya lives in Seattle", about=["Maya", "Seattle"])]), today=T)
    assert len(store.memories()) == 2, log

def test_a_wording_match_about_the_same_entities_is_reinforced(store, monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr(store_module, "DUPLICATE_SCORE", 0.0)
    store.apply(Extraction(**MAYA_BOSTON, memories=[mem("Pytest's sister Maya lives in Boston", about=["Maya", "Boston"])]), today=T)
    log = store.apply(Extraction(**MAYA_BOSTON, memories=[mem("Maya, Pytest's sister, lives in Boston", about=["Maya", "Boston"])]), today=T)
    assert log[-1].startswith("reinforced"), log

def test_a_vetoed_nearest_does_not_hide_an_allowed_match(store, monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr(store_module, "DUPLICATE_SCORE", 0.0)
    store.apply(Extraction(**MAYA_BOSTON, memories=[mem("Pytest's sister Maya lives in Boston", about=["Maya", "Boston"])]), today=T)
    store.apply(Extraction(entities=[EntityOut(name="Maya", kind="person")],
                           memories=[mem("Pytest's sister Maya is a nurse", about=["Maya"])]), today=T)
    # nearest by wording is the Boston memory (vetoed: Boston isn't named); the nurse one is allowed
    log = store.apply(Extraction(entities=[EntityOut(name="Maya", kind="person")],
                                 memories=[mem("Pytest's sister Maya lives in Boston", about=["Maya"])]), today=T)
    assert log[-1].startswith("reinforced") and "nurse" in log[-1], log

def test_dropping_an_entity_on_a_re_read_stores_a_copy(store, monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr(store_module, "DUPLICATE_SCORE", 0.0)
    store.apply(Extraction(**MAYA_BOSTON, memories=[mem("Pytest's sister Maya lives in Boston", about=["Maya", "Boston"])]), today=T)
    store.apply(Extraction(entities=[EntityOut(name="Maya", kind="person")],
                           memories=[mem("Pytest's sister Maya lives in Boston", about=["Maya"])]), today=T)
    assert len(store.memories()) == 2

def test_repeats_about_other_entities_in_one_extraction_are_both_kept(store, monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr(store_module, "DUPLICATE_SCORE", 0.0)
    store.apply(Extraction(entities=[EntityOut(name="running", kind="activity"), EntityOut(name="swimming", kind="activity")],
                           memories=[mem("Pytest went running", "event", about=["running"]),
                                     mem("Pytest went swimming", "event", about=["swimming"])]), today=T)
    assert len(store.memories()) == 2
```

Note: `test_a_vetoed_nearest...` is a positive-control test, so it reinforces even with the cut at 0. With the veto, the Boston memory is excluded and the nurse memory (about {Maya} ⊆ {Maya}) is the only candidate.

- [ ] **Step 2: Run them to verify they fail**

Run: `uv run pytest -q tests/test_09_write_path.py -k "wording_match or vetoed_nearest or dropping_an_entity or repeats_about"`
Expected: `test_a_wording_match_about_other_entities_is_new`, `test_dropping_an_entity...` and `test_repeats_about_other_entities...` FAIL (one memory, reinforced or skipped). `test_..._same_entities_is_reinforced` PASSES (a control). `test_a_vetoed_nearest...` FAILS (it reinforces the Boston memory).

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement the veto in `companion/store.py` `_apply`**

- Before the tombstone check, compute `about_ids = {eid for n in mem.about if (eid := self._lookup(n, known)) and eid != self.user}`.
- Repeat check: `stored` holds `(vec, about_ids)`. A stored entry counts only if `its_ids <= about_ids`.
- Index query: pass `about=sorted(about_ids)` and add to the WHERE, before `RETURN ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1`:
  `AND all(x IN [(node)-[:ABOUT]->(e) WHERE NOT e:User | e.id] WHERE x IN $about)`
- The "new" log line: `[new: nothing similar with the same dates and entities]` when `nearest` is empty.
- The later `about` list for CREATE is unchanged (it still defaults to `["user"]`).

- [ ] **Step 4: Run the tests to verify they pass, plus the existing write-path tests**

Run: `uv run pytest -q tests/test_09_write_path.py tests/test_14_production.py tests/test_18_inspect.py`
Expected: all pass, including `test_a_repeated_memory_gains_the_entities_it_names` and `test_duplicate_memory_is_reinforced_not_copied`.

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add companion/store.py tests/test_09_write_path.py
git commit -m "Veto a duplicate match when the old memory is about other entities"
```

### Task 2: Tombstones carry entities

**Files:**
- Modify: `companion/store.py` (`forget`, `_tombstones`, the tombstone check in `_apply`)
- Test: `tests/test_09_write_path.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: `about_ids` from Task 1.
- Produces: `Forgotten.about: list[str]`. `_tombstones(episode_id) -> list[tuple[np.ndarray, set[str]]]`.

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_a_tombstone_only_blocks_memories_about_its_entities(store, monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr(store_module, "FORGOTTEN_SCORE", 0.0)  # wording says "the forgotten one" for anything
    ep = store.start_episode(on=T)
    store.apply(Extraction(entities=[EntityOut(name="Jordan", kind="person"), EntityOut(name="Denver", kind="place")],
                           memories=[mem("Pytest's ex Jordan moved to Denver", about=["Jordan", "Denver"])]), ep, T)
    [m] = store.memories()
    assert store.forget(m["id"])
    log = store.apply(Extraction(entities=[EntityOut(name="Denver", kind="place")],
                                 memories=[mem("Pytest is moving to Denver next year", about=["Denver"])]), ep, T)
    assert [x["text"] for x in store.memories()] == ["Pytest is moving to Denver next year"], log
    log = store.apply(Extraction(entities=[EntityOut(name="Jordan", kind="person"), EntityOut(name="Denver", kind="place")],
                                 memories=[mem("Jordan, Pytest's ex, moved to Denver", about=["Jordan", "Denver"])]), ep, T)
    assert len(store.memories()) == 1, log
```

Expected: FAIL at the first assertion (the Denver move was skipped as "a memory the user asked to forget").

**Files:**
- Modify: `companion/store.py` (the guard at about line 518 in `_apply`)

input.recap: I committed the follow-up spec and plan as 6194f4f on structure-over-prose. They cover the entity veto for duplicates and forget tombstones, plus a trip guard that reads expiry instead of kind. Nothing is implemented yet, and the LLM test run is still going.

content.text:
The follow-up plan is written and committed as `6194f4f` on `structure-over-prose`. Nothing is implemented yet.

- **Spec:** [structural-matching-design.md](docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-06-structural-matching-design.md)
- **Plan:** [structural-matching.md](docs/superpowers/plans/2026-11-06-structural-matching.md), 4 tasks

**What it changes.** Merging two different memories loses data, while wrongly splitting one memory into two only leaves a near-copy. So the graph gets a veto over wording matches. An old memory can match a new one only if every entity the old one is about (other than the user) is also in the new one. That one rule covers three places:

1. **Duplicate detection.** "Maya lives in Boston" can no longer reinforce "Maya lives in Seattle" and lose the move. "Went running" can't swallow "went swimming".
2. **Repeats within one extraction.** Two memories from the same message about different entities are both kept.
3. **Forget tombstones.** Forgotten memories now record which entities they were about. After forgetting "Jordan moved to Denver", "I'm moving to Denver" is no longer dropped. Old tombstones without that record behave as they do today.

The trip guard is a separate small fix. It now treats any memory with an expiry as temporary, not just ones labelled `status`.

The tests make the similarity cut match anything, so the entity veto alone decides the outcome. They'll behave the same on any embedding model.

**What I left out, and why:**
- **Entity matching:** I downgraded it after reading the code. It already tries the extractor's id first, then an exact name. Its fallback needs both similarity checks to agree, and the "one mother" rule already merges by graph structure. That's less exposed than I said in my last answer.
- **Sensitive-recall floor:** recall is supposed to be fuzzy.
- **The "step" word check:** fixing it needs an ontology change.

**One limit:** two memories about only the user ("likes coffee" / "likes tea") still depend on wording alone, as they do today. The spec states this.

The plan should run after the current branch, since it relies on activities being entities.

The LLM test run is still going. Its output so far shows 12 failures in a row. That could be the expected extraction-model check failing in every scenario, but I won't know until it finishes and I can read the failure details.

def about_entity(run: Run, name: str, word: str, relation: str | None = None) -> list[dict]:
    """Current memories ABOUT an entity named `name` (optionally with this relation to the user)
    whose text contains `word`."""
    return run.q(
        """
        MATCH (m:Memory {user: $user})-[:ABOUT]->(e:Entity {name: $name}) WHERE m.invalidated_at IS NULL
          AND toLower(m.text) CONTAINS toLower($word)
          AND ($rel IS NULL OR EXISTS { (:User {id: $user})-[r:RELATED {type: $rel}]->(e) })
        RETURN m.id AS id, m.text AS text, m.due_on AS due_on
        """,
        name=name, word=word, rel=relation,
    )

The LLM run finished. These are its results and what I've done since:

- **The gym habit now forms.** The check that started all this ("three gym visits became one lasting habit") passes on gemini-3.8-flash.
- **13 of the 14 scenario failures were the extraction-model check.** Each of those failed only because the thresholds were recorded against gemma, which is expected. I've now set `extraction_model` to `gemini-3.8-flash`.
- **One real failure, and it was the test's fault.** "The wedding is dated 2027-06-12" failed even though the extraction was right: it stored "Priya is getting married." with `due_on` 2027-06-12. The check only looked at memories containing the word "wedding". It now looks for a memory about Priya with that date, whatever the wording. I recorded this as a ruling in the ledger. The cost if I'm wrong is that a different Priya memory due that same day would also pass.
- **Fast suite: 226 passed, 4 skipped.**

The LLM scenarios are re-running in the background with both changes. If they come back clean, I'll commit "Re-measure thresholds on gemini-3.8-flash" and then run the final branch review with a fresh reviewer.

              SET m.consolidated_at = $now MERGE (p)-[:SUMMARIZES]->(m)
              RETURN count(CASE WHEN NOT had THEN 1 END) AS added
            }
            SET p.evidence = coalesce(p.evidence, 0) + added
            """, now=now, pattern=pattern_ids, ids=[r["id"] for r in members])''')
s=s.replace('''habit). Occurrences only (event, status, plan, feeling)''','''habit), and plans alone are no habit until something happened. Occurrences only (event, status, plan, feeling)''')
open(p,"w").write(s)
EOF

A background job runs after every conversation (`close_episode`) and from `/consolidate`:

1. **Lapse.** Open plans more than 14 days past due become `lapsed`, so the extractor stops
   seeing them as candidates.
2. **Roll up.** An activity (an `activity` entity such as "gym") with occurrence memories
   (events, statuses, plans, feelings from the last 60 days) `ABOUT` it on **3 or more
   distinct days** is a habit. Its memories go to a small LLM step,
   `extract.find_pattern()`, which writes one lasting memory or declines. The pattern is
   `ABOUT` the activity, the user gets a `practices` link to it, each member gets a
   `SUMMARIZES` edge and a `consolidated_at` stamp, and the pattern's `evidence` is the
   number of memories it summarizes. Once an activity has a pattern, later days attach to it
   as more evidence, without asking the LLM for a new sentence.
3. **Prune.** Delete dormant memories with importance ≤ 3 that have **expired** (`valid_until`
   has passed), but only once they're rolled up or older than the 60-day window. Events stay
   as history even when dormant: they have no `valid_until`.

    doesn't, future plans aren't days yet, a known habit gathers evidence without a rewrite;
  - pruning only expired, dormant trivia;
  - plans lapse;

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/markcastillo/Library/Application Support/Claude/local-agent-mode-sessions/4b164a4a-f885-4be8-bb7c-2a0b87072585/473e3f37-a4d9-4625-a90c-00c4adb97e89/rpm/REDACTED/skills/finishing-a-development-branch

# Finishing a Development Branch

## Overview

**Core principle:** Verify tests → Detect environment → Present options → Execute choice → Clean up.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the finishing-a-development-branch skill to complete this work."

## Step 1: Verify Tests

Run the project's full test suite (`npm test` / `cargo test` / `pytest` / `go test ./...`).

**If tests fail**, report the failures and stop — the menu comes after a green suite:

```
Tests failing (<N> failures). Must fix before completing:

[Show failures]
```

**If tests pass:** continue to Step 2.

## Step 2: Detect Environment

```bash
GIT_DIR=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
GIT_COMMON=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
# Capture now, while still inside the workspace — Step 5 changes directory
# before cleanup (Step 6) needs this value
WORKTREE_PATH=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)
```

This determines which menu to show and how cleanup works:

| State | Menu | Cleanup |
|-------|------|---------|
| `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON` (normal repo) | Standard 3 options | No worktree to clean up |
| `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, named branch | Standard 3 options | Provenance-based (see Step 6) |
| `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, detached HEAD | Reduced 2 options (no merge) | Externally managed — leave in place |

## Step 3: Determine Base Branch

The base branch is whatever this work forked from — usually named in the
plan, the conversation, or the branch's upstream. If it is not already
known, ask: "This branch split from <your best guess> - is that correct?"
Confirm before merging: merging into the wrong base is expensive to undo.

## Step 4: Present Options

**Normal repo and named-branch worktree — present exactly these 3 options:**

```
Implementation complete. What would you like to do?

1. Merge back to <base-branch> locally
2. Push and create a Pull Request
3. Keep the branch as-is (I'll handle it later)

Which option?
```

**Detached HEAD — present exactly these 2 options:**

```
Implementation complete. You're on a detached HEAD (externally managed workspace).

1. Push as new branch and create a Pull Request
2. Keep as-is (I'll handle it later)

Which option?
```

Present the menu exactly as written — concise, with every option coming
from the list above. Discarding the work happens only in response to your
human partner explicitly asking for it (see "If your human partner asks to
discard the work" below). Wait for their answer; the integration decision
is theirs.

## Step 5: Execute Choice

### Option 1: Merge Locally

```bash
# Get main repo root for CWD safety
MAIN_ROOT=$(git -C "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/.." rev-parse --show-toplevel)
cd "$MAIN_ROOT"

# Merge first — verify success before removing anything
git checkout <base-branch>
git pull
git merge <feature-branch>

# Verify tests on merged result
<test command>
```

If tests fail on the merged result: stop, leave the worktree and branch in
place, and investigate — nothing has been pushed, so the merge is local
and recoverable.

Once the merged result is green: clean up the worktree (Step 6), then
delete the branch:

```bash
git branch -d <feature-branch>
```

### Option 2: Push and Create PR

```bash
git push -u origin <feature-branch>
# From a detached HEAD, name the new branch on the remote:
# git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/<new-branch>
```

Then create the pull/merge request against <base-branch> with the forge's
tooling — its CLI if one is available, or the creation URL most forges
print when you push — following the repo's PR template and conventions if
present, and report the URL to your human partner.

Keep the worktree — your human partner iterates on PR feedback there.

### Option 3: Keep As-Is

Report: "Keeping branch <name>. Worktree preserved at <path>."

### If your human partner asks to discard the work

This path exists only as a response to an explicit request to throw the
work away. Confirm first:

```
This will permanently delete:
- Branch <name>
- All commits: <commit-list>
- Worktree at <path>

Type 'discard' to confirm.
```

Wait for that exact confirmation. When it arrives:

```bash
MAIN_ROOT=$(git -C "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/.." rev-parse --show-toplevel)
cd "$MAIN_ROOT"
```

Then clean up the worktree (Step 6) and force-delete the branch:

```bash
git branch -D <feature-branch>
```

## Step 6: Cleanup Workspace

**Runs for Option 1 and confirmed discards.** Options 2 and 3 always
preserve the worktree. Both callers have already changed directory to the
main repo root — worktree removal must run from outside the worktree —
and use the `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_COMMON`/`WORKTREE_PATH` values captured in
Step 2, from before that directory change.

**If `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON`:** Normal repo, no worktree to clean up. Done.

**If `WORKTREE_PATH` is under `.worktrees/` or `worktrees/`:** Superpowers
created this worktree — we own cleanup:

```bash
git worktree remove "$WORKTREE_PATH"
git worktree prune  # Self-healing: clean up any stale registrations
```

**If removal is refused** (`contains modified or untracked files`): the
worktree holds files that exist nowhere else — uncommitted plans, notes,
or scratch work. Never `--force` on your own initiative. Show your human
partner what is at stake and ask:

```bash
git -C "$WORKTREE_PATH" status --porcelain -uall
```

```
Worktree removal refused — these files were never committed:

<file list>

1. Commit them to <branch> before cleanup
2. Move them into <main repo root>
3. Delete them (unrecoverable)

Which?
```

Carry out the choice, then remove the worktree.

**Otherwise:** The host environment owns this workspace — leave it in
place. If your platform provides a workspace-exit tool, use it.

## Quick Reference

| Option | Merge | Push | Keep Worktree | Cleanup Branch |
|--------|-------|------|---------------|----------------|
| 1. Merge locally | yes | - | - | yes |
| 2. Create PR | - | yes | yes | - |
| 3. Keep as-is | - | - | yes | - |
| Discard (explicit request only) | - | - | - | yes (force) |

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Tests passed earlier this session" | Run the suite on the tree you are about to integrate. A green run only proves the tree it ran on. |
| "They obviously want it merged" | Integration is your human partner's decision. Present the menu and wait. |
| "They seem done with this feature — I'll offer to discard it" | The menu is complete as written. Discard happens only when your human partner asks for it in so many words. |
| "'Yeah, get rid of it' counts as confirmation" | Only the typed word `discard` authorizes deletion. |
| "The PR is up, so the worktree is clutter now" | PR feedback gets fixed in that worktree. It stays until the work lands. |
| "This other worktree looks stale — I'll clean it too" | Clean up only worktrees under `.worktrees/` or `worktrees/`. Everything else belongs to the host. |
| "Removal refused — `--force` is just finishing the cleanup" | The refusal means files exist only in that worktree. `--force` destroys them permanently. Show your human partner and ask. |
| "The merged-result failure is probably flaky" | A failing merged result stops everything. Branch and worktree stay put while you investigate. |
| "The base branch is obviously main" | Confirm the fork point or ask. Merging into the wrong base is expensive to undo. |
| "The push was rejected — force-push will fix it" | A rejected push means the remote moved. Investigate; force-push only on your human partner's explicit request. |
